articles.title: Judge orders Kinew government to disclose who excluded Tesla from Manitoba EV rebate program and why
articles.summary: A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric-vehicle…

image.caption: A Tesla showroom is puctured in Surrey, B.C., on March 19, 2025 — the last day Tesla vehicles qulified for EV rebates in Manitoba. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric-vehicle rebate program — and explain why that decision was made.
'Exceptional and unusual' step taken by judge following 'baffling coyness' from provincial government

A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric vehicle rebate program — and explain why that decision was made.

In an order issued Nov. 13, Court of King's Bench Justice Elissa Neville gave Wab Kinew's government 10 days to produce "a complete record" of the decision-making process that disqualified anyone who purchased Tesla vehicles after March 19, 2025, from qualifying for Manitoba's EV rebates.
This means the NDP government has until Monday to explain the decision, which Tesla initially asked the court to overturn in May.

For the past six months, Tesla has argued the decision was unreasonable, untransparent and unfair because, the company contends, it's not clear who actually decided to exclude Tesla from the EV rebate program and whether that person was legally authorized to make that decision.
The government, in turn, has argued the exclusion can not be reviewed in court because it was a funding decision.

items: Tesla asks court to overturn exclusion from Manitoba EV rebate program

blocks.text: In her order, Neville said she can not make any determination without knowing who made the decision and said the NDP government has displayed "a baffling coyness" about the decision-making process.

"The disputed record filed with the court sheds no light whatsoever on the question of who made the Tesla exclusion decisions, how they made the decisions, why they made the decisions, and whether these decisions are reviewable," Neville wrote.
"The respondents' position, in effect, appears to be that the reviewability of the decision must be determined before they can identify the decision maker and produce the record."
The judge went on to note it is not routine for courts to order governments to disclose the rationale behind decisions.
"I acknowledge that compelling the respondents to file their record by way of an affidavit is an exceptional and unusual remedy," Neville wrote.

"That said, in the specific and unique circumstances of this case, where the respondents refuse to identify anyone as the decision maker, such an approach strikes me as the more practical and efficient means of ensuring that there is a clear and streamlined record before the court."
Rebates yanked on budget day 2025

Manitoba's EV rebate rolled out in 2024 but was retroactive to 2023. It entitled Manitobans buying a new electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid priced below $70,000 to a $4,000 rebate. Used and leased EVs qualified for a $2,500 or $1,000 rebate, respectively.

On provincial budget day in 2025, Finance Minister Adrien Sala said removing Tesla from the EV rebate was about "Trump-proofing our economy" and a "commitment to be elbows up." Chinese EVs were also excluded at the time.
Manitoba Finance Minister Adrien Sala speaks to reporters on March 20, 2025, when he unveiled a provincial budget that excluded Tesla from EV rebates. (Jaison Empson/CBC)
Tesla argued this exclusion ran counter to the stated purpose of the EV rebate program and also cost consumers $560,000.

items: Tesla's exclusion from Manitoba EV program 'incredibly unfair,' politically motivated, court hears

blocks.text: During a court hearing in October, Tesla's legal counsel noted Premier Wab Kinew said in 2025 that Tesla CEO Elon Musk should "get Donald Trump to stop the tariffs, and then we can talk about the EV rebate."

In her order, Justice Neville voted "in the absence of a proper record, the applicant says it has only media reports and public remarks from Manitoba's Premier through which to glean the rationale for the Tesla exclusion decision.
The province, she noted, considered the EV rebate change to be a policy decision made under the government's spending power.

"The applicant is entitled to seek to challenge a decision affecting its interests. The respondents intend to argue in this case that the decision the applicant challenges is not reviewable because it is a policy decision," she wrote.

"I cannot make that determination without knowing who the decision-maker was. For some reason, the respondents are saying that it is for the court to make that determination, even though the respondents have neither taken a position nor provided the information necessary for me to do so."
A motion by the government to strike the Tesla application will be heard at the same time as the application, Neville said.
Tesla's Winnipeg legal counsel declined further comment.
The NDP government declined comment as well.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation. He's the author of three books — two of them Canadian bestsellers — and the winner of a Canadian Screen Award for reporting.

articles.title: Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds
articles.summary:
Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators

The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven…

blocks.text: The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said.
The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.

Lynch, 59, had been enjoying a voyage around Sicily with family and friends after his acquittal in a long-running fraud case regarding the sale of the technology company he founded, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard in 2011.

He and his 18-year-old daughter, Hannah, died, as did lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife, Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife, Judy, and the yacht’s chef, Recaldo Thomas. Nine other crew members and six guests were rescued.

blocks.caption: Hannah and Mike Lynch were among the seven people who died when the yacht sank. Photograph: Family Handout/PA

blocks.text: The MAIB final report, published on Thursday, appears to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecutors have reportedly blamed errors by the crew.

The MAIB report details how the yacht was hit “by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast” of about 70 knots (80 mph), which knocked it on to its side in less than 15 seconds. It sank 18 minutes later.

Investigators found that the yacht’s vulnerability to strong winds had never been assessed for the conditions in which it was anchored, with its sails down and its retractable centreboard raised. The centreboard is a large underwater structure that helps a sailing vessel remain stable.
The extreme weather was most likely caused by a downburst – a powerful blast of air from a thunderstorm that hits the sea and spreads out with enormous force, the report said.

None of the life rafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel. The crew managed to release one manually. Survivors were rescued by crew from a nearby yacht, the Sir Robert Baden-Powell.

Rob Loder, the chief inspector of MAIB, said: “This accident developed with extraordinary speed. In just 14 minutes, calm conditions had given way to winds of at least 68 knots, which in less than 15 seconds pushed the yacht on to its side.

blocks.caption: The crew of the Bayesian ‘had no warning of the risk’, said the chief inspector at MAIB, Rob Loder.  Photograph: MAIB/PA

blocks.text: “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down. The extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk.”

The report conveys the desperate minutes as the Bayesian was knocked down. Crew were alerted by sudden and severe winds of up to 30 knots at 03.55, and within two minutes the yacht listed starboard and the vessel began to drag anchor before the wind suddenly increased to about 70 knots.

“At 04.06 Bayesian violently heeled over 90 degrees to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on,” the report said.
after newsletter promotion

Some guests, awoken by the listing and who had left their cabins, escaped. One couple used furniture drawers as an improvised ladder. Guests who managed to get to the flying bridge were instructed to swim away from the vessel and warned to stay clear of the mast and boom as it sank.

blocks.caption: Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking into the deaths of Judy and Jonathan Bloomer, 71 and 70 respectively, as well as of Mike and Hannah Lynch.  Photograph: Family handout/PA

blocks.text: Passengers and crew who made it out gathered in the water, using a torch on a mobile to search for others. A crew member managed to swim back to the yacht to manually release one life raft from stowage. By 04.24 the life raft was inflated.

The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.

It said information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast also did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms it predicted, it said.
Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking at the deaths of Mike and Hannah Lynch and Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, who were all British nationals.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court resumes Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Thursday, with the defense set to present four government officials as witnesses.

On Day 44, the proceedings will test whether the defense can address the prosecution’s allegations of P817.17 million in unexplained wealth, questionable business transactions involving a company linked to her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, and Duterte’s financial disclosures.
WATCH: Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Nov. 19, 2026

items: The witnesses are former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) investigator Rainer Dela Fuente, Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, Food and Drug Administration Director IV Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan, and Center for International Expositions and Missions (Citem) department manager Rowena Mendoza.
The witnesses are expected to discuss financial investigation rules, company registration and business transactions involving Cale88 Food Corp., allegedly partly owned by Carpio.

The prosecution maintains that Duterte and Carpio accumulated at least P817.17 million in unexplained wealth. Forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera’s broader assessment indicated that potentially undisclosed assets could exceed P1.5 billion.
The defense previously presented explanations involving a P205,007 dinner in Tokyo, Japan, and a P256,882.50 Nike shoe purchase in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, both charged to Carpio’s credit card./dp

articles.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 US per share, valuing AI giant at $1.51 trillion US
articles.summary: Anthropic has set a stock price of $83 US per share for its hotly anticipated initial public offering, with shares of the U.S. artificial intelligence giant set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange on…

image.caption: Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January 2025. ((AP Photo/Markus Schreiber))

blocks.text: Business

Anthropic has set a stock price of $83 US per share for its hotly anticipated initial public offering, with shares of the U.S. artificial intelligence giant set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday.
What you need to know about the company as it prepares to debut on Nasdaq

Anthropic has set a stock price of $83 US per share for its hotly anticipated initial public offering (IPO), with shares of the U.S. artificial intelligence giant set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday.

At $83 US per share, Anthropic, the company behind the popular Claude chatbot, is valued at approximately $1.51 trillion US, a figure that includes unvested employee stock options and other promised shares.
This surpasses the $70 to $78 US range from Anthropic's Nov. 10 regulatory filing. In a news release Wednesday, the company also upsized its offering by 155 million shares.
The debut valuation is massive compared to anything in Canada, representing more than a quarter of the combined market value of every company listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

items: Anthropic IPO to test the first 'pure play' AI stock in a choppy market

blocks.text: The money raised in the offering alone exceeds every major Canadian IPO combined over the past 30 years.
Ernest Wong, head of research at Toronto-based Baskin Wealth Management, notes that Anthropic dwarfs the most valuable company on the TSX, Royal Bank, which is currently worth $377 billion.

"That really speaks to the global nature of large U.S. tech companies today," he told CBC News on Wednesday. "These are large companies that touch every aspect of our lives, and the revenue and valuation reflect that."

The $83 US per share IPO price announced on Wednesday is the price paid by institutional investors and retail buyers who secured pre-IPO allocations through participating brokers. The actual market price will be determined after trading is underway on Thursday.
The company's ticker symbol is "ANT."
Inside Anthropic’s trillion-dollar IPO gamble | About That
Here's what you should know about the company and its stock market debut.
What is Anthropic?

Anthropic started as a niche AI research lab in 2021. Its founders left rival OpenAI because they felt that company was too focused on profits, ignoring risks and giving too much control to investors.

The company gained momentum in 2024 when it released the Claude 3.5 Sonnet chatbot. This version beat OpenAI's GPT-4o on major performance benchmarks at a fraction of the cost of previous frontier AI models.

Unlike other tech giants like Apple or Microsoft, Anthropic is not a traditional for-profit company. It's organized as a public benefit corporation, meaning its board has a legal mandate to balance public safety against maximizing shareholder returns.

items: AI industry needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up, Anthropic CEO says

blocks.text: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is a leading advocate for AI safety, arguing the industry should slow development to let safety measures catch up.

"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," he said at a United Nations Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence in September.
Anthropic CEO calls for AI development to slow down
When does Anthropic start trading?
Under Nasdaq's listing and trading rules, newly listed shares do not begin trading immediately after the 9:30 a.m. ET opening bell.
Nasdaq temporarily holds the stock in a price-discovery auction, giving the exchange and bankers leading the sale time to match incoming bids and offers into an opening price.
Some Canadian brokerages, like Wealthsimple and major bank platforms, had options for everyday investors to request shares in advance at the fixed offer price, prior to the Nasdaq auction.
However, the supply of shares is often limited, and investors may face holding restrictions or penalties for selling right away.
How Anthropic's IPO creates a single 'God share' | About That
What do we know about Anthropic's financial performance?
Anthropic lost $42 billion US in 2025, according to regulatory filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
In the first nine months of this year, the company booked an $104 billion US net loss. However, this was largely driven by non-cash accounting charges tied to its soaring pre-IPO valuation.

Meanwhile, sales have been brisk. In the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic generated $33.24 billion US in revenue — a 1,206 per cent increase year-over-year. Its annualized sales pace hit roughly $81 billion US in October.

Anthropic also has big spending plans. Unlike Google or Microsoft, Anthropic has historically rented its computing power rather than owning physical data centres. It's locked into roughly $450 billion US in long-term computing and data-centre commitments through 2030.
How are Anthropic's peers trading?
Since Anthropic is laser-focused on building and selling AI models, its shares are seen as a unique "pure play" on the artificial intelligence boom.
That sets it apart from most stocks associated with AI, which typically have other businesses.
Take Google's parent company Alphabet, for example. It's considered an AI "hyperscaler," but it has a massive suite of non-AI businesses, like YouTube and Android smartphones.
AI-related stocks have been on a roller coaster lately, swinging between panic-driven sell-offs and relief rallies.

items: The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
AI stock sell-off sends the S&P 500 down 4.4% in worst day since April 2025

blocks.text: Shares of companies like Oracle, Microsoft, and Amazon saw massive gains through the summer and early fall. Since then, a trio of headwinds have emerged: the leadership crisis at Nvidia; U.S. regulators putting tighter controls on China's access to AI chips; and fears of a data centre slowdown in the U.S. driven by the "blue wave" of Democrat victories in the recent midterm elections.
As a result, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index is down nearly seven per cent over the past month.
Wong says investors buying Anthropic stock should brace for big price swings early on. He says his firm does not typically buy IPOs, and will take a wait-and-see approach.
"I think it's [going to be] very volatile," Wong said. "It really takes some time before the trading of the stock kind of settles into where it's supposed to be."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI released as gamers rejoice globally
articles.summary: After 13 years of waiting, fans around the world will get to play the latest installment in the blockbuster video game series. In focus: A tale of crime and violence in a fictionalized version of…

image.caption: GTA VI is released after more than a decade of developmentImage: Silas Stein/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI will be officially launched Thursday, ending a 13-year wait for one of the most anticipated games ever.

The game will become playable at midnight local time (CET) on a wide range of platforms, including PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, meaning gamers in Asia will get to play the game ahead of users in the US and Europe.
In New Zealand, one of the first countries worldwide where the game became available, the release prompted internet providers to prepare for a spike in internet usage at midnight.
This comes due to the game's size of 212 gigabytes, more than a quarter of the average New Zealand household's usage in a month.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA franchise, faces high expectation after 13 years of anticipation, with previous versions having become commercial and cultural hits around the world.
GTA games sold 470 million units worldwide, and the fifth installment generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days after its release in 2013.

blocks.caption: Jason and Lucia's experiences are at the center of GTA VIImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: GTA's global success
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' parent company, saw its shares rise by more than eight percent the day before the game's release.
The game takes place in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami.

It follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple drawn into criminal networks while trying to secure a better life. GTA games are often criticized for including excessive violence and for glorifying crimes and drug use.
Lucia, a former prisoner, and Jason, an ex-military man, experience a series of criminal jobs that go wrong in the drug-trafficking world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida.
According to Rockstar, Leonida is the company's most detailed open world so far, extending beyond Vice City into smaller communities and nightlife hotspots inspired by locations in South Florida.
Music has been an intrinsic part of the GTA experience, and the latest game is expected to feature a soundtrack including artists like Tame Impala and SZA.

articles.title: After 3 days in detention, ASEAN protesters ordered released
articles.summary: Prosecutors dismissed complaints of malicious mischief and alarms and scandals for lack of evidence.

blocks.text: November 19, 2026 | 7:57am
Protesters march during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on November 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — After three days in detention, more than 200 protesters arrested during an ASEAN-related rally in Muntinlupa City were ordered released on Wednesday, although they still face preliminary investigation over several complaints.
In a resolution dated November 18, the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office dismissed complaints of malicious mischief and alarms and scandals against the protesters for lack of prima facie evidence.
Senior Assistant City Prosecutor Elvin Keith Barrios, however, referred the remaining complaints for further preliminary investigation.

These include alleged violations of Batas Pambansa 880, or the Public Assembly Act, and provisions of the Revised Penal Code on resistance and disobedience to a person in authority and grave coercion.
Barrios also denied a motion filed by the National Union of Peoples' Lawyers seeking the dismissal of all complaints against the protesters.

"The remaining charges were referred for further preliminary investigation where the respondents may submit counter-affidavits and evidence in support of their defenses," Department of Justice spokesperson Polo Martinez said.
All 20 minors released
In a message to reporters Wednesday evening, Martinez said the police had referred 233 individuals to the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office, including 213 adults and 20 minors.
Citing the prosecutor's office, Martinez confirmed that all 20 minors had been released.
Prosecutors also dismissed the complaints against six children below the age of 15, who were released to the custody of their parents or legal guardians for appropriate intervention.

"OCP Muntinlupa also ordered the release of all other respondents pending the conduct of preliminary investigation as to the remaining charges. In view of that order, it deemed the request by respondents for immediate release moot," Martinez said.
More than 200 protesters were arrested in separate demonstrations across Metro Manila on Sunday, November 15, as regional leaders gathered for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit.

The arrests drew condemnation from human rights organizations, lawmakers and members of the clergy, with several groups calling for the protesters' immediate release and investigations into alleged police abuses.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: [Puso at Diwa] A lost opportunity to test the truth in Sara Duterte’s trial
articles.summary: The withdrawal of witnesses may be a tactical decision for the defense. But for the Filipino people, it is also a lost opportunity to test the truth.

blocks.text: There is something unsettling about a trial in which witnesses initially identified by one side suddenly disappear from the witness stand.

The defense of Vice President Sara Duterte has withdrawn 18 of the 24 witnesses it initially listed before the Senate impeachment court. Among them were 16 bank executives from eight financial institutions, including BPI, BDO, LandBank, Metrobank, PSBank, Security Bank, EastWest and UnionBank. Other witnesses, including former law dean Ralph Sarmiento and Quezon City Prosecutor Vimar Barcellano, were also dropped.

blocks.caption: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial

blocks.text: The defense has legitimate procedural reasons for doing so.

Some testimony, it said, was no longer necessary or could be covered by stipulation. In the case of BPI senior vice president Paul Roderick Ysmael, counsel explained that his purpose was merely to authenticate a letter whose authorship had already been acknowledged in open court. The testimony of Prosecutor Barcellano was likewise dispensed with after the prosecution agreed to stipulate to the authenticity of the public documents he was expected to identify. (READ: [Puso at Diwa] Foreign currency deposit secrecy: Time for a constitutional rethink)
The defense has that prerogative.

But an impeachment trial is not an ordinary dispute between private parties. It is a constitutional proceeding involving one of the country’s highest elected officials. Ultimately, it is the Filipino people who must live with the consequences of the Senate’s judgment.
That is why the withdrawal of witnesses deserves attention beyond courtroom strategy.
A witness may help the defense, hurt the defense, or reveal something neither side expected. That is precisely why witnesses are examined and cross-examined.
The most consequential example appears to be the BPI witness.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] A lost opportunity to test the truth in Sara Duterte’s trial

blocks.text: The prosecution wanted to question Ysmael about bank records and an alleged dollar account involving the Vice President. Prosecutors cited a BPI letter indicating that Duterte had dollar accounts and said they wanted to clarify the records and circumstances surrounding them. But the witness was withdrawn before they could ask those questions.

That matters because the prosecution has raised a much larger financial issue. Financial forensic expert Alexander Cabrera reportedly placed the Vice President’s alleged unexplained wealth at a minimum of ₱817 million. Yet, according to the prosecution, the defense had not directly challenged that computation by the end of Day 43. Instead, it presented testimony concerning a ₱205,007 Tokyo dinner charged to the credit card of Manases Carpio and a ₱256,882.50 Nike shoe purchase in Kuala Lumpur.
Those explanations may be relevant. But they do not, by themselves, answer the larger question surrounding the alleged ₱817 million.
And this is where cross-examination becomes indispensable.
The truth is not always found in the testimony one side wants the public to hear. It is often found in the questions the other side is allowed to ask.
The defense may reasonably conclude that certain witnesses are unnecessary, redundant or even unhelpful. It is not required to present every witness it initially identified.
But once a witness is withdrawn, the opposing side loses the opportunity to test that witness’s testimony and explore matters that documents alone may not resolve.
This does not mean that the withdrawal proves guilt.
It does not.

Nor should the prosecution automatically treat every withdrawn witness as evidence that its allegations are true. Ralph Sarmiento, for example, reportedly declined to testify because he wanted to preserve his independence and impartiality, a reason that deserves respect.
But neither should the withdrawal be treated as inconsequential.
The issue is not whether the defense has violated a rule. It appears not to have done so. The issue is whether the country is being given the fullest reasonable opportunity to discover the truth.
That distinction is important because an impeachment proceeding is ultimately about accountability.

If the prosecution’s allegations are weak, let the defense demonstrate why. If the ₱817 million computation is wrong, let the evidence expose the error. If the alleged dollar accounts have an innocent explanation, let the relevant records and witnesses establish it. And if the allegations are substantiated, let the evidence demonstrate that as well.
The answer to a serious allegation should not be less scrutiny. It should be more scrutiny.

This is also why the withdrawal of 18 witnesses, three-fourths of those initially listed, creates a credibility problem, even if it does not establish wrongdoing. House prosecution panel leader Gerville Luistro noted that the withdrawals could create an impression that witnesses did not want to be identified with the party that intended to present them. She also acknowledged that expectations had been raised for a strong defense presentation.
But public perception should not substitute for evidence.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks

blocks.text: The proper response is not to assume that the withdrawals prove anything. It is to recognize what the withdrawals prevent: the fullest possible testing of evidence before the court.
And that is ultimately what should concern us.

We have seen too many political controversies in which truth becomes hostage to competing narratives, partisan loyalties and social media. One side tells its story, the other tells its story. Each mobilizes its supporters, and the public is left asking what actually happened.
An impeachment trial should rise above that.

It should be one of those rare moments when politics gives way to evidence—when witnesses testify, documents are examined, claims are challenged, contradictions are exposed, and senators ultimately decide on the basis of what survives scrutiny.
That is what gives the Senate verdict legitimacy.
If the Vice President is acquitted, the Filipino people should know that the prosecution failed to establish the charges after the evidence was fully tested.
If she is convicted, they should likewise know that the conviction was not the product of political persecution but the consequence of evidence that survived rigorous examination.
In either case, the process matters as much as the outcome.

A conviction reached after a full and fair examination of the evidence strengthens the rule of law. An acquittal reached after the same process strengthens the credibility of the accused and of the institution that rendered the judgment.
But a verdict that leaves material questions unanswered inevitably leaves room for doubt.
This is why the withdrawal of witnesses should concern not only the prosecution but everyone who cares about truth, justice and democracy.
The defense is entitled to manage its case. But the Filipino people are entitled to expect that every reasonable avenue for establishing the truth will remain open.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] A lost opportunity to test the truth in Sara Duterte’s trial

blocks.text: Let the witnesses speak when their testimony is material. Let the prosecution cross-examine them. Let the defense explain and rebut. Let the documents be tested. Let contradictions surface. Let the evidence, not the volume of political rhetoric, determine the judgment.
For if the ultimate result is conviction, the nation must know that it was earned by evidence, not manufactured by politics.
And if the result is acquittal, the nation must know that the allegations were given a full and fair hearing and were found wanting.
Either way, the country wins when the truth is allowed to speak.

The withdrawal of witnesses may be a tactical decision for the defense. But for the Filipino people, it is also a lost opportunity to test the truth. And in an impeachment proceeding of this magnitude, every lost opportunity to test the truth is an opportunity lost for justice, accountability and democracy itself. – Rappler.com

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.
He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

articles.title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for $1.4tn stock market debut
articles.summary: Anthropic started just five years ago an is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.

blocks.text: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of at least $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.
It will be the first US company focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry.
The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is considered a true AI company, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products for consumers and businesses.
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.

It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is built on expensive, reliant on in-demand computer chips, controversial data centres, and deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

Xi, Trump, Putin exchange greetings before historic China summit
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia exchanged greetings as they met in Shenzhen on Wednesday, a day before their history-making first formal trilateral summit in the Chinese city.
The agenda for Thursday's meeting between presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin -- which has raised fears of a carve-up into new "spheres of influence" -- was unclear, however.

When Trump touched down in Shenzhen, Xi became the first Chinese paramount leader in decades to welcome a foreign leader as he arrived, mirroring the US president's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September.
Trump descended the stairs from his plane to be met by Xi, as well as renditions of both countries' national anthems and fighter jets that flew overhead and left colorful vapor trails.

articles.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine
articles.summary: The suspect followed employees and and was found with fake US ID documents and two Russian passports, US prosecutors say.

blocks.text: US investigators have arrested a Russian man who they say was recruited by Moscow to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm in California's Silicon Valley that has links to Ukraine.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a spying operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco.
He is also accused of stalking employees of the company and possessing falsified identity documents.

The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia. US prosecutors say the company was targeted by Russia due to its assistance to Kyiv.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, the company in question is Palantir Technologies. Palantir did not reply to a BBC request for comment.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

articles.title: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
articles.summary:
First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday…

blocks.text: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

articles.title: How the NBI foiled an alleged school shooting plot in Ilocos Norte
articles.summary: The foiled shooting plot in Ilocos Norte comes amid growing concerns over school safety. This year alone, three deadly school shootings occurred between June and September 2026.

blocks.text: Trigger warning: Mentions of shooting, killing, and death
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) foiled an alleged school shooting plot involving three minors in Batac, Ilocos Norte, NBI Director Melvin Matibag revealed recently.
The planned attack was reportedly scheduled for December 16, 2026 — coinciding with the start of Simbang Gabi or the dawn Masses associated with Christmas.
One of the minors had reportedly experienced bullying since Grade 7 and was influenced by video of the 1999 Columbine High School shooting in the United States.
“Nakakuha kami ng report from our counterparts abroad sa NBI. May isang group na nakita sila nag-uusap. Immediately we deployed ang task force natin,” Matibag said in an interview with ABS-CBN News.
(We received a report from our counterparts abroad. They discovered a group of individuals discussing [the planned attack]. We immediately deployed our task force.)
On November 17, the NBI disclosed that three 16-year-old students were suspected of planning a shooting attack against their schoolmates in Batac, Ilocos Norte.
According to Matibag, one of the students allegedly intended to target students who, he claimed, had bullied him since the 7th Grade.

During interviews with investigators, he identified several individuals whom he accused of bullying.According to a South China Morning Post report, the teenager reportedly recruited two other students to participate in the plan. The two, however, thought that the proposed attack was a joke.

The plot came to the attention of Philippine authorities after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) discovered an online group chat. The suspected students allegedly discussed the planned attack in their conversation.

Following the tip, the NBI then deployed its Task Force on National Violent Extremism to investigate the report, as Matibag explained. Authorities subsequently conducted operations in Batac on November 15 and 16, leading to the three teenagers being taken under the bureau’s custody.
Matibag confirmed that the statements obtained from the minors during interviews were consistent with the information given by the FBI.

Aside from the reported bullying, investigators identified a possible influence in the planned attack. According to Matibag, the Grade 9 student who initiated the plot had watched videos of the 1999 Columbine High School shooting in the US.
“Napanood niya ang video ng Columbine, which encouraged him to do the same,” Matibag told reporters.
(He watched a video of the Columbine [shooting], which encouraged him to do the same.)

The Columbine High School shooting occurred on April 20, 1999, in Colorado. During the attack, two students opened fire and killed 12 students and one teacher. Around two dozen others were injured before the attackers took their own lives.
At that time, Columbine received extensive media coverage and prompted widespread concerns about school safety.

The shooting became a reference point for subsequent attacks. Research examining school shootings found that some perpetrators had studied the Columbine incident or explicitly referred to it when planning their own attacks.
The foiled shooting plot in Ilocos Norte comes amid growing concerns over school safety. This year alone, three deadly school shootings occurred in the Philippines between June and September 2026.

items: On June 22, three students were killed at San Jose National High School in Tacloban, Leyte. Two minors aged 14 and 15 were identified as suspects in the attack.
Another shooting happened on August 18 at Ateneo de Zamboanga University. A Grade 9 student shot and killed a Grade 10 student before taking his own life.
On September 18, shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato left three students dead. Among those killed was the 16-year-old suspected gunman.

blocks.text: Apart from these incidents, authorities have recorded several school shooting threats and suspected plots. Between June 16 and August 19, the Philippine National Police recorded 12 shooting threats involving schools nationwide.
Interior Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla said in October that law enforcement officials had also thwarted 53 other suspected shooting plots in South Cotabato. – Rena Eñano/Rappler.com
Rena Eñano, a Rappler intern, is a senior literature student from Ateneo de Manila University.

articles.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
articles.summary: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondent
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military's operations in 2017

blocks.text: Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military's operations in 2017

The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.

She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.

Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.

When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.

Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Aung San Suu Kyi's refusal to condemn the Myanmar military's actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers

blocks.text: Aung San Suu Kyi's refusal to condemn the Myanmar military's actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.

"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.

"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.

That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.

The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar

blocks.text: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."

He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.

Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

articles.title: GTA 6 bedazzles gamers in Australia with ‘fully lived in, breathable world’
articles.summary:
Players can renovate houses, fix cars, lift weights and follow the story in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Miami-inspired Vice City

Gamers across Australia woke up Thursday morning feeling like…

blocks.text: Gamers across Australia woke up Thursday morning feeling like Christmas came early, some bleary-eyed from late night sessions on the Playstation, others with grand plans for a weekend foray in Vice City when their day jobs let them loose.

Grand Theft Auto VI, more than a decade in the making, is here. And the reviews, mere hours into release, reflect universal acclaim. The game has already vaulted to the top spot on Metacritic’s list of the best games of all time, sitting above 1998’s The Legend of Zelda, Ocarina of Time with an unprecedented 99/100 score.
Australians who put in a few hours as soon as the game launched at 12am said they were already beyond impressed.
“I had it loaded up bang on midnight,” Pat, 26, told Guardian Australia. “I just got on straight away, it was like being a kid on Christmas morning.”

He spent about two hours exploring the world of Leonida and its metropolis – based heavily on Miami – and his initial thoughts echoed others who described the GTA VI release as the “moon landing” of gaming.
“This is a fully lived in, breathable world. It’s so much more tangible than so many video games,” Pat said. “I was at a loss for words trying to express to my girlfriend how significant this is.”

Angus, 27, has the game downloaded and ready to play but had to be at work today, “which is unfortunate”. He and two friends have developed a detailed plan involving pizzas, beer and hour-long shifts on a shared TV on Thursday night into the early hours of Friday morning.

“The last one came out when I was pretty much in grade 8,” he said. “I just turned 27, and the hype hasn’t really gone at all. It’s the only game where I’ve genuinely felt excited, it’s like Christmas morning to be honest.”
“I’m just really keen to get home and play it,” he added. “Hopefully the work day goes quick.”
He took Friday off to get in as much time as he could, with the trio planning to pass the controller around between power naps.
Maggie Brennan, an online creator who streams under the banner retromaggie on Twitch, said the game had been fantastic so far.

“The graphics are beautiful, from the texture of the pores in the character’s skin to the air blowing through their hair. Rockstar have done an amazing job,” she said. “But that water! That water is beautiful.”

She said just hours in there was already an untold level of detail for players to interact with. Gamers can renovate their houses, fix their cars, lift weights and follow the story, all buttressed by Rockstar Games’ “unhinged madness that we all love”.
Up in Sydney, Pat said he plans to fit in GTA VI around his work schedule as much as possible, with the whole weekend already written off for time in Vice City.
“I was supposed to have a work event on tonight and it got cancelled,” he said, temporarily hopeful. “But it’s back on now. The amount of sorrow I felt…”
“I might have to work from home tomorrow,” he added. “I think the light rail might not be running properly…”

articles.title: First Nations health watchdog investigating how Sask. boy lost use of small intestine after routine surgery
articles.summary: Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.

image.caption: First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond, right, and Kristen Lerat, centre, speak to media in Saskatoon on Wednesday. (Chanss Lagaden/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sask. Health Authority also conducting internal review
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost the use of his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sheldon OneBear Rosebluff, 4, is now in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon. He requires a small intestine transplant.
On Wednesday, his family and First Nations leaders held a media event to discuss the case and ongoing concerns about how Indigenous people are treated by the provincial health-care system.

First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond said she launched an investigation into Rosebluff's medical ordeal after the boy's family filed a complaint. Lafond said she can't discuss the details of Rosebluff's situation until the investigation is complete.

"Nothing is black and white and some cases are very complex," Lafond said on Wednesday. "When a child goes in for a simple procedure and will now be in the health-care system for years … you've got a lot of different factors at play."
The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) confirmed it is conducting its own review of the care Rosebluff received in hospital.

items: FSIN appoints ombudsperson to investigate racism in health care

blocks.text: Kristin Lerat is Rosebluff's biological aunt and has been his caregiver for about three years. She described Rosebluff as a talkative boy who likes to build forts, dance and drum.
"A happy, energized boy. And this has taken the richness out of not only his life, but our lives too," Lerat said.
In September, Rosebluff had a successful surgery in Regina for appendicitis. He appeared to be recovering well until Oct. 24, when he suddenly turned ill and was taken back to hospital, Lerat said.

He had a blockage in his bowels and required surgery. After two surgeries in Regina within days, he was airlifted to Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon, where he eventually had two more surgeries over the course of a week.
"He was critical the whole time, but his body just couldn't handle that many surgeries," Lerat said.
Something happened that "killed" his small intestine and he now requires a transplant, Lerat said.
Sheldon One Bear Rosebluff, 4, seen here in an undated photo prior to his medical ordeal. (Submitted by Kristen Lerat)
The SHA declined to comment on Rosebluff surgeries and his condition due to privacy legislation.
But the SHA is conducting a review of the care Rosebluff received and "what might have occured," according to a statement emailed to CBC.

"Patient safety and the delivery of high-quality, patient-centred care remain top priorities for the SHA, and we take patient safety concerns very seriously," SHA chief medical officer Dr. Rashaad Hansia said in the statement.

"Social Work supports are in place to assist in liaising with the family and coordinating with partner agencies, and we are commit[ted] to ensuring these interactions and supports are provided in a culturally respectful way."
Lafond did not provided a timeline for the ombudsperson investigation, but said more details will be released once it is complete.
Cowessess First Nation Chief Erica Beaudin attended the media event to support the Lerat family.
"We are not here to denounce the health-care system or the people in it," Beaudin said.
"What we're talking about is how we must recognize when we must do better.… For us, treaty is not a land acknowledgement. It is action."
The First Nations Health Ombudsperson is an independent office established by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations to investigate complaints about the health-care system.

In October 2025, the ombudsperson said her office had received about 500 complaints since opening in 2023. About 64 per cent of the cases derived from complaints and issues associated with the services of the Saskatchewan Health Authority.

The boy's family is also concerned about being sidelined for important medical decisions. Lerat said the social services ministry took over decision-making for Rosebluff's care once the boy's condition turned critical.

"It was me and the doctors making the decisions. Now it's the ministries and the doctors making decisions," Lerat said. "So if we get a doctor that does not believe in our traditional ways, what does that look like?"
The Ministry of Social Services provided a statement to CBC.
"Due to provisions in The Child and Family Services Act, the Ministry of Social Services is unable to confirm involvement with a family or speak to specific details of any case," it said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.

articles.title: MLB commissioner says owners won't compromise on salary cap, leaving sport headed to lockout
articles.summary: Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred says team owners will not move off their demand for a salary cap, leaving the sport on track for a lockout starting Dec. 2 that could threaten the 2027…

image.caption: Baseball's five-year collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. A lockout, which would be the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972, would bring to a halt all trades and signings. (John Fisher/Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB

Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred says team owners will not move off their demand for a salary cap, leaving the sport on track for a lockout starting Dec. 2 that could threaten the 2027 season.
'Competitive balance is a serious problem, and it needs to be addressed'
"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," he said Wednesday at a news conference during an owners meeting in New York.
Players say they will never accept a cap. The last time management proposed a cap in 1994, it led to a 7 1/2-month strike that caused cancellation of the World Series for the first time in 90 years.

"There's plenty of room for compromise, but there's one thing that I will not compromise and that's the issue that we're hearing from the vast majority of our fans: They want a salary cap and floor and on that we will not compromise," Manfred said. "We are not prepared to tell 70 per cent of our fans that they're wrong on this issue.
“Competitive balance is a serious problem, and it needs to be addressed and it's one that we can't avoid just because the negotiation may be difficult."

Baseball's five-year collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. A lockout, which would be the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972, would bring to a halt all trades and signings.

"A decision on a lockout is one that we're going to make at the last possible moment," Manfred said. "We're going to devote ourselves to the bargaining process. I'm not that big on Thanksgiving as a holiday. We'll make ourselves available whenever and wherever to bargain in an effort to make an agreement."

items: MLB teams face tough calls on signings, trades as current labour deal runs out

blocks.text: MLB proposed the sport adopt a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028 and a floor of $180.2 million, using luxury tax payrolls with average annual values. A team would be allowed to remain as low as 90 per cent of the floor in 2028, which would be $162.18 million, but would have to spend the entire amount of the floor over a three-year period.
Individual contracts also would be capped under the plan, which MLB says includes a 50-50 split of revenue. The union takes issue with management's definition of revenue and expenses.
MLB to MLBPA: 'This proposal is serious'
Players have called the salary cap a "non-starter."
"We made the proposal way back in May. Another word for 'non-starter' over months is a refusal to bargain," Manfred said.

"I think it's time that the MLBPA needs to realize that this proposal is serious. I'm not suggesting they need to accept it whole cloth. I think they need to look at the proposal and try to find some ways to move to the middle as opposed to making no proposal at all."

items: Shorter regular season among drastic changes MLB proposes to players
MLB owners propose salary cap to players for 1st time since baseball's 1994-95 strike

blocks.text: Players proposed a "competitive integrity tax" that would penalize teams dropping below a payroll floor. They also asked for a rise in the luxury tax threshold and increased salary arbitration rights.
"The MLBPA wants more and its proposals undermine, further undermine the competitive quality of our game," Manfred said.

"What has the MLBPA done? They've engaged in a lot of rhetoric," he added. "They've characterized our proposals as not real or not serious. They've criticized and mischaracterized aspects of the cap and floor system to promote player opposition. What the MLBPA has not done is made any meaningful effort to move towards us.
“In fact, they have not made a significant economic proposal since their opening proposal. Indeed, there's a paucity of responses even on topics that do not directly impact our economics."

articles.title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences
articles.summary:
Von der Leyen says she wants to give Kyiv ‘strong hand’ in talks and is confident all 27 member states will back idea

The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to…

blocks.text: The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues.

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
She expressed confidence all 27 member states would stand behind the loan, despite four central and eastern European countries having already ruled themselves out.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he hoped for the swift adoption of the loan and was counting on the support of all EU member states: “Strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end,” he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy convinced EU leaders last month that his country faced a €70bn funding gap in 2027. The EU pledged to cover €45bn and wants Ukraine’s other allies to cover the rest.

Only 11 months ago, the EU agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, which was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s military and civilian needs in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia’s attacks have escalated, the cost of Ukraine’s defence and the toll of economic disruption continue to rise.

Andrius Kubilius, the EU defence commissioner, said Ukraine’s military spending was increasingly dominated by drones. Ukraine, he told reporters, expected Russia to use 10m drones this year and 20m in 2027. “Ukraine with EU assistance needs to match – and will match,” he said.
The EU loan is split into two parts: €25bn for weapons and €20bn for civilian needs, including funding essential services, such as schools and hospitals.

Von der Leyen expressed confidence that all member states would support the loan because “all 27 member states say very clearly that they want to support Ukraine”. She said member states could choose to support Ukraine’s civilian needs, rather than military spending.

Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, however, have said they do not intend to take part in the latest funding round for Ukraine, prompting a warning from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, that he would block the EU’s seven-year budget unless all countries got onboard.
The four central and eastern countries are net beneficiaries of the EU budget, while Germany is the largest payer and Ukraine’s biggest EU donor.
The EU wants Ukraine’s non-EU allies – such as Norway, the UK and Canada – to find €25bn for Kyiv in 2027.

The EU proposal included provisions “to help other countries to help us”, a senior commission official said. Brussels has proposed that G7 countries that provide new loans get guarantees that the borrowing can be repaid with future profits from Russia’s frozen assets.
The profits from the Russian assets are being used to repay a €45bn loan issued by the G7 to Ukraine in 2024.
after newsletter promotion

Countries with a triple-A credit rating could opt to provide guarantees to the EU budget up to €5bn to expand European borrowing for Ukraine on capital markets. The commission has identified six countries that fall into this category: Australia, Canada, Liechtenstein, Norway, Singapore and Switzerland.

EU officials previously said the UK and other allies needed to do more to support Ukraine in 2027, arguing that the EU was shouldering too much of the burden. The UK subsequently pledged a £10bn economic and military support package for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said: “The UK, Canada, Japan, and Norway have been helping tremendously in our defence of life, and establishing clear rules under which they can provide further aid in conjunction with the EU will help even more.”

Britain said on Wednesday night it would send 1,000 long-range attack drones to Ukraine as part of a further £260m military aid package, a day before prime minister Andy Burnham was due to travel to Berlin to co-chair a meeting of Kyiv’s European allies.

The commitment to support Ukraine’s deep strike campaign into Russia emerged a day after the US argued that Kyiv’s attacks on refineries and warehouses were ineffective and counter-productive, earning criticism from the UK and Germany.
“The UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself,” Burnham said.
