articles.title: Birmingham council granted interim ban on union jacks on lamp-posts
articles.summary:
High court judge issues order against Raise the Colours over flags on council-owned street furniture

The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks…

blocks.text: The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks on lamp-posts and roundabouts in Birmingham after a legal challenge by the local council.

The high court judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction banning the placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture without prior permission in a judgment issued on Wednesday, Birmingham city council said.

The council, run by a minority coalition led by the Liberal Democrats, sought the injunction against seven people identified as supporting or participating in the affixing of flags in the city, including Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of Raise the Colours and “persons unknown”.

The application for an injunction, which attracted national attention and follows similar action by Oxfordshire county council, argued the actions of the flag activists had caused danger, alarm and distress.

People associated with Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, have been placing union jacks and St George’s flags on public infrastructure across the country since August last year.

The group’s website states it is a “campaign to cover Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism”. However, others have accused the group of racism and spreading anti-immigration rhetoric – claims it has previously denied.
In its claim to the high court, Birmingham city council said the defendants had travelled across the city “unlawfully affixing flags” and had confronted residents who attempted to remove them.
“In doing so, they are engaging in tortious and criminal behaviour, which is both antisocial and dangerous,” the claim read, adding that the behaviour had caused “danger” and “alarm” to residents.
The council said residents of Birmingham had suffered “fear, anxiety, intimidation, harassment,” been put at “serious risk of harm”, and some had suffered physical injuries, including a broken leg.

The case was adjourned in early September after the judge said she was “troubled by the lack of clarity” from the council “against the individual defendants”, and a further hearing was scheduled at the end of September.
Bridge opposed the injunction and read a written statement to the court. He said: “For me, the union flag represents home, identity, belonging, national identity, British culture and patriotism.”
His lawyer, Liam Wells, argued that the injunction would have a “chilling effect” on human rights and that erecting union jacks and St George’s flags was an expression of his political views.
Wells said the interim injunction would risk “silencing people in their political views and expression of political opinions” and the council had failed to prove Bridge had acted unlawfully.

Three local residents, Adam Biggs, Mark Hudson and Tony Kaye, joined the case representing ‘persons unknown’ opposing the injunction bid, and expressed concerns it would ban people flying flags for pride and other campaigns.
The council’s cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, said on Wednesday the local authority was grateful for the judgment and it was an “important step”.

“We have taken a proportionate and evidence-led approach throughout this case. Our priority has always been to protect public safety, supporting the welfare of our staff and contractors, maintaining community cohesion and ensuring public funds are used responsibly,” she said.
In a video uploaded to Facebook, Bridge said he was “gutted” and “devastated” by the decision, including the fact that the injunction granted power of arrest against him and others.
He said Raise the Colours was “not about race, colour, creed” but about opposing “illegal invaders breaking in our country, jeopardising our borders, on the rubber dinghies”.
At the Reform UK conference in Birmingham in September, Nigel Farage promised to help Bridge in his legal fight if the party was able to do so.

In response to the judgment, Reform’s leader in Birmingham, Jex Parkin, said the council had its “priorities entirely wrong” and had pursued an “ideologically driven case against residents proudly displaying our national flags – at huge public expense”.

The leader of the local Conservatives, Robert Alden, also criticised the injunction and said the council was “punishing ordinary Birmingham residents who simply want to show pride in where they live”.
He said: “Amidst a 23-month bin strike, loss of roads funding, and mounting litter on our streets, the council has chosen to make this court action a priority.”

The group Brummies United Against Racism, which campaigned for the injunction, welcomed the judgment. Members of the group told the Guardian earlier this year they had presented evidence of incidents involving Raise the Colours to the police and council officers.

The group said it was “not opposed to this country’s flag” and many of its supporters “see the flag as a symbol of celebration and unity”. “However, we are firmly opposed to those who seek to use the flag to further an agenda of hate and who dress up racism as patriotism,” a statement read.
A further hearing in the case will take place on Thursday.
Additional reporting by PA

articles.title: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine's latest strike on the Kerch Bridge has disrupted a key transport link between Russia and Crimea. Beyond the damage, the attack could have serious consequences for Russian military logistics…

image.caption: Debris from the destroyed bridge arch is obstructing the main shipping route linking the Black Sea and the Sea of AzovImage: Ukrainian Security Service/AFP

blocks.text: It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.

Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.

Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.

The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.

It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
A long time in the making

The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.

blocks.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin (center) personally oversaw the bridge's constructionImage: YURI KOCHETKOV/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink. There has been no confirmation of this so far.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea
The impact on shipping

After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.

Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."

As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.

Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
The military consequences
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."

Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.

Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."

blocks.caption: The bridge's road-traffic arch has collapsed into the seaImage: Ukrainian Security Service/AFP

blocks.text: That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
A bad look for Putin

Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China.

Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."

Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."
Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."
"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: PlayStation suffers widespread network problems hours before release of GTA VI
articles.summary:
Disruption comes at critical moment, with Grand Theft Auto VI one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in history

PlayStation has suffered widespread network problems just hours before the…

blocks.text: PlayStation has suffered widespread network problems just hours before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in recent gaming history.
The disruption emerged Wednesday, causing frustrated players to flood social media with complaints about failed logins and server connection problems downloading games and updates.
PlayStation’s official network status page acknowledged problems affecting its gaming and social services, which has left players struggling to access online features.
“You might have difficulty launching games, apps, or network features. We’re working to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Thank you for your patience,” the alert read.

Many affected users said their internet connections were working normally, suggesting the problems were specifically affecting PlayStation’s online services. Some PS5 owners said that their consoles successfully completed internet connection tests, only for the “Sign in to online services” check to fail.
The scale of the disruption was reflected on Downdetector, a website that tracks real-time service outages, which cited 1,228 user reports of PlayStation outages by Wednesday afternoon.

The website monitors disruptions using reports submitted by users, with sudden spikes potentially indicating that large numbers of people are experiencing similar technical difficulties. The reports do not independently confirm the extent of an official outage, however.

Although no official cause has been established, the timing of the problems has raised questions about whether the issue could be linked to a recently released PS5 software update. Sony announced Tuesday evening that it had rolled out a system software update required for users planning to play GTA VI.
Sony’s official troubleshooting advice recommends that affected players examine their system software and internet connections.
The disruption comes at a critical moment for PlayStation users, with GTA VI scheduled to launch at midnight Thursday.

GTA VI is being lauded as the most anticipated game in history. The hype for the latest installment of the iconic GTA franchise, the first new game in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has already suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game.

articles.title: Women's rugby players fight to save team after Bishop's University cuts varsity program
articles.summary: Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, Que., has decided to cut its women’s varsity rugby team. The news comes as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world, and university varsity teams are a…

image.caption: The Gaitors are the women's varsity rugby team at Bishop's University. The players were told this week that the school will be cutting its varsity status after this academic year is over. (Courtesy of Bronwyn Chénard)

blocks.text: Montreal

Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, Que., has decided to cut its women’s varsity rugby team. The news comes as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world, and university varsity teams are a pipeline to fuel the national team roster.
Some players had moved across the country to join team, were blindsided by decision

Women’s rugby players at Bishop's University in Sherbrooke, Que., say they were left in tears and shock when they were told on Monday the team would no longer receive varsity support or funding beyond this school year.
According to the university, the decision was taken by its board of governors following a year-long review.
“It really felt like being stabbed in the chest,” said Tessa Brosseau, who moved from Vancouver to attend the university in Quebec’s Eastern Townships.
"The reason that I'm at Bishop's is because of Bishop's women's rugby,” said the fourth-year student. “It means everything. It means my life.”
Claudia Croteau and Abigail Burns, both rookies from Alberta, also moved across the country to play for the varsity rugby team.
Bishop’s University drops women's rugby and men's lacrosse — blindsiding athletes

The young women say they think of each other as family now, bonded together by all the hard work and sacrifices they've each made to be part of the team — including countless hours of training during early mornings, late nights and rainy practices.
Fighting to keep their rugby dreams alive
The school suggested the team could continue as a club. But the players don’t see that as an equivalent replacement.
“None of us came here to play club rugby,” said Brosseau. “We came here to potentially be prospects for the national program."

Universities with a varsity team can be a pipeline to get onto the national roster. The prospect of that is particularly appealing to young female athletes now, as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world.
Being a varsity team means more amenities, as well, including access to coaching and medical staff. It's also the last level before being able to play professionally.
LISTEN | Women's rugby team not giving up on keeping varsity status:
Quebec AM11:10Bishop’s University rugby players speak out against decision to cut varsity program
The players are not willing to let go of that dream without a fight.
They’ve launched an online petition that’s garnered more than 6,000 signatures, and are considering fundraising in hopes of reversing the board’s decision.
If a solution can’t be found, Croteau admitted that she and other rookies are contemplating transferring schools as a last resort, in order to be able to still play rugby at the varsity level.
“Yes, we love Bishop’s,” she said, “but what makes Bishop’s so amazing is rugby."
'Women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear'
In its explanation of the decision to cut the varsity program, the university acknowledged it was facing “significant financial pressure.”

However, the team says it was never consulted to help address that challenge. Nor has it been informed of what criteria was considered when taking the decision, which the university has said is final.
Rylee Fletcher, who’s in her fourth year at Bishop’s, is hoping to bring wider attention to what she calls a "devastating" decision.
“At a time when women’s sports are gaining long-overdue recognition, investment, and support, it is incredibly discouraging to see opportunities for female athletes being taken away,” she said.
“We believe women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear.”
The team finished last this season, but the players believe the future of the team is still bright. (Courtesy of Bronwyn Chénard)
Bishop’s University has said the school has chosen to concentrate its resources on fewer varsity teams to better support their needs.

"This decision reflects financial and operational sustainability, competitive fit and the resources each sport requires. It does not diminish the value of women’s rugby or the people who play it," a school representative said in an emailed statement.
Bishop's plans to keep four women’s and four men’s varsity teams. They include both basketball and golf teams, as well as men’s football and rugby, and women’s hockey and soccer.
Men's lacrosse team also cut
In addition to Bishop's women's varsity rugby team, the men’s varsity lacrosse team has also been cut.

The Canadian University Field Lacrosse Association (CUFLA) said in a statement that it hasn't officially been notified of the decision, but considers it to be a "significant setback" to its efforts of reversing the trend of Canadian student athletes choosing American universities to pursue their education and lacrosse careers.

The CUFLA says it has noticed a "significant increase" in Canadian student athletes returning from universities in the U.S. over the past several years to continue their pursuits at Canadian institutions.
"Lacrosse is increasingly becoming a driver of university enrolment, making the decision by Bishop's University particularly difficult to understand," the CUFLA said.

items: McGill may reinstate track and field program next year

blocks.text: Last year, McGill University cut 25 club and varsity teams across 15 sports, including women’s rugby.
Concordia is now the only English-language university with a varsity women’s rugby team in Quebec.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Patricia Kozicka is a digital journalist with CBC Montreal. She has previously worked in Toronto and Edmonton. You can reach her at patricia.kozicka@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Kwabena Oduro and Quebec AM

articles.title: Hegseth boasts about Maduro’s capture while vowing to deepen US military cooperation with Venezuela
articles.summary:
The US defense secretary called the former president’s capture the ‘most sophisticated military operation’ in Latin American history

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since…

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

articles.title: Competition Bureau examining marketing practices by Gap, Old Navy
articles.summary: The Competition Bureau is moving ahead with an investigation into whether clothing giants Gap and Old Navy are violating marketing regulations by making potentially false or misleading claims in…

image.caption: An Old Navy location is seen in the Greater Toronto Area. Canada's competition watchdog is looking into the marketing practices of both Gap and Old Navy stores. (David MacIntosh/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

The Competition Bureau is moving ahead with an investigation into whether clothing giants Gap and Old Navy are violating marketing regulations by making potentially false or misleading claims in their advertising.
Probe focusing on whether regular prices are inflated when items are on sale and the use of urgency cues

The federal Competition Bureau is moving ahead with an investigation into whether clothing giants Gap and Old Navy are violating marketing regulations by making potentially false or misleading claims in their advertising.

The competition watchdog has been granted a court order for information it says will help it determine whether the retailers are supplying customers with genuine regular prices when advertising items as on sale.
It is also examining the retailers' use of so-called urgency cues — messages such as ''Selling Fast'' or ''Only a Few Left'' — that pop up on their sites while consumers are browsing.

items: When is a deal really a deal? We tracked prices at Old Navy and Canadian Tire to find out

blocks.text: Old Navy and Gap are both owned by Gap Inc. and operate both online and bricks and mortar stores nationally.
CBC News has reached out to Gap Inc. for comment about the investigation.

The bureau says it took action after it saw a surge in complaints last year about allegedly inflated regular prices. At the time, it published a warning to remind businesses of their obligations under the Competition Act.
It adds that its ongoing investigation has yet to find any instances of wrongdoing.
Old Navy clothing sales are just regular prices, customers allege

articles.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth signs military deal in Venezuela
articles.summary: On a visit to Caracas, Pete Hegseth signed a deal that signifies the "reestablishment of our defense partnership." US-Venezuela ties were strained for years until US troops ousted ex-President…

image.caption: Hegseth spoke with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez during the visit Image: Miraflores Palace/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.
What do we know so far about Hegseth's trip?
The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.

The visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, US President Donald Trump has backed acting President Delcy Rodriguez to lead the country.

blocks.caption: Hegseth also met with new Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, who had belonged to a party opposing Maduro  Image: Miraflores Palace/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Both Rodriguez and Hegseth touted the new military agreement between the two countries at the presidential palace in Caracas.
Rodriguez said the deal would strengthen training for the Venezuelan military while facilitating access to new technologies. She said this would allow the two nations to "face common threats."
Hegseth said the US sees the deal "as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries."
The agreement includes intelligence sharing between the two nations in addition to joint training.

The Pentagon chief said the US seeks "to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders."
Hegseth said Wednesday that since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."
How have US-Venezuela relations changed?

US-Venezuela relations were strained under Maduro, who had taken office in 2013. In 2019, Maduro cut off Venezuela's formal diplomatic relations with the US after Trump's first administration recognized Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido as the country's interim president.
Is the US looting Venezuela?

After the ouster of Maduro, the Trump administration urged Venezuela to comply with demands such as US access to the Venezuelan oil market. Trump had threatened Rodriguez, who was Venezuela's vice president, with a "fate worse than Maduro" if she didn't cooperate with Washington.
Trump has later praised Rodriguez as a "terrific person" who is doing a "great job."

Under Rodriguez, Venezuela has released political prisoners and facilitated the shipments of oil to the US, with the US then controlling the proceeds and returning the money under an energy deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been overseeing Venezuela's transition and is in close contact with Rodriguez.

Elections after Maduro's ouster are expected at some point in Venezuela, but with Rodriguez's government acting favorably towards the US, it's unclear whether they would happen anytime soon. Nobel Prize winner and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently urged elections after arriving in Venezuela.

articles.title: What it will take for Canada to regain its measles elimination status
articles.summary: The U.S., Bolivia and Mexico lost their measles elimination status this week, as Canada did this time last year. What would it take for Canada to regain its status?

image.caption: Signs in English and Low German warn of a measles alert at the Taber Community Health Clinic in Taber, Alta., on July 28, 2025. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Health·New
The U.S., Bolivia and Mexico lost their measles elimination status this week, as Canada did this time last year. What would it take for Canada to regain its status?
Experts say re-eliminating the preventable, sometimes deadly disease is important — and well within reach
The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles elimination status this week, following in Canada's footsteps.
Last November, Canada lost its measles elimination status after 27 years, during a two-year outbreak that infected more than 6,400 people. The outbreak was declared over on Oct. 19.

items: The U.S. has officially lost its measles elimination status amid worst outbreak in 35 years
At 'crucial' moment for pandemic preparedness, experts say world isn't ready

blocks.text: Regaining Canada's measles elimination status is well within reach, experts say — and crucial, given the health risks from the highly contagious, sometimes deadly and completely preventable disease.

In addition to fever and rash, about one in three people with measles will have one or more complications, including diarrhea, ear infections that can lead to permanent hearing loss, pneumonia, inflammation of the brain or seizures.

In the Canadian outbreak, two infants died — one in Alberta and one in Ontario — when they contracted measles in the womb and were born prematurely. Ten people have died in the U.S. so far this year, The Associated Press reports.
The U.S. has officially lost its measles elimination status

Jennifer Nuzzo, a professor of epidemiology and director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health in Rhode Island, told CBC News Tuesday that other countries that have regained their status show a path forward for the U.S. and Canada.

Venezuela and Brazil, for instance, "got vaccine rates up, they engaged with communities, they improved their surveillance, and they were able to regain their measles elimination status," Nuzzo said. "So it shows us that it's possible to turn things around."
Here's what it would take to restore Canada's measles elimination designation:
12 consecutive outbreak-free months

There are multiple criteria for earning measles elimination status. At its most basic level, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) requires one year without residents spreading the disease to declare a country measles-free. Canada lost its elimination status last year because its outbreak continued for more than 12 months.

items: Confirmed measles case in Durham region: unimmunized child with history of recent international travel
Surge in measles cases risks 'horrific' health consequences: immunologist

blocks.text: Elimination doesn't require zero measles cases, but rather no outbreaks with continuous transmission from the same strain of the virus.
In a statement Tuesday, PAHO noted that Canada "has interrupted the chain of transmission" and is working to regain elimination status.
An action plan

PAHO, which is the regional arm of the World Health Organization, says countries must submit a corrective action plan outlining the strategies and measures they will implement, and then prove they have stopped the transmission of the outbreak strain for at least 12 months.
When Canada lost its status, PAHO said the country would present an action plan "focused on boosting immunization coverage, reinforcing surveillance systems, and ensuring rapid outbreak response."
The Public Health Agency of Canada's 2025-26 departmental results report also details in broad strokes a "Measles Action Plan for Canada".

Trudy Dyck, a community health representative at Alberta Health Services, takes part in a course related to the measles outbreak, at the Taber Health Centre in Taber, Alta., in October 2025. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)
95 per cent vaccine coverage

To achieve no ongoing outbreaks for 12 months, countries need a vaccination rate of about 95 per cent, experts say. At that rate, communities achieve herd immunity, which can protect those unable to be vaccinated, such as infants.

In recent years, Canada has been well below 95 per cent. A 2025 study estimated 92 per cent coverage with one dose, but found only 79 per cent received the recommended two doses of the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella vaccine.

"No matter who's in power in Canada or the U.S., what administration, political left, right, it doesn't matter, because what is important is the vaccination rates among the population," said Dr. Alon Vaisman, an infection control physician at Toronto's University Health Network.
Education of skeptical communities
Vaisman said the vaccination numbers he sees show transmission is likely occurring in pockets where there are low vaccination rates, rather than evenly across the whole population.

The Canadian outbreak, which began at a gathering in New Brunswick, was concentrated in some provinces within close-knit religious and culturally distinct communities, including Mennonite populations in Alberta and Ontario.

items: Addressing fear in Alberta's Mennonite community amid a measles outbreak
Canada's measles outbreak control challenged by disinformation and distrust, doctors say

blocks.text: "So the work required to get back to elimination means investing and educating pockets of the population in Canada, U.S., to increase their vaccination rates," Vaisman said. He added that education should be non-judgmental and speak plainly about side effects.
"Luckily, the vaccine has very few, and basically no long-lasting, side effects," he said.

Dr. Lynora Saxinger, an infectious diseases specialist at the University of Alberta, said when Canada lost its status last year that countering organized disinformation about vaccine safety would require a formal, organized resistance. That includes making debunking videos and looking closely at how algorithms shape disinformation.
Trump signs executive order calling to reduce childhood vaccinations
Nuzzo told CBC News that proper outreach takes a "ground game" — being out in communities and engaging with trusted leaders to explain why the vaccine is important and how severe the disease is.
Increased surveillance
Close surveillance is critical for measles elimination, PAHO says.

There have long been calls for Canada to improve surveillance of infectious diseases — especially given cuts to U.S. health institutions that could result in increased transmission across the border. Experts have called for timely collaboration across provincial and territorial boundaries.

After the loss of status, PHAC said online it is working with provinces, territories and other vaccination partners to enhance monitoring activities, and that it is "improving the quality of Canada's measles surveillance system."
CBC News has reached out to the Public Health Agency of Canada for more specifics about the surveillance improvements and other steps Canada has taken to regain elimination status.
With files from Tashauna Reid, Amina Zafar, Alexandra Mae Jones, The Canadian Press, The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.summary: Hamas condemns the incursion, which the Israeli military says is dismantling a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.

blocks.text: Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Parks Canada budget cuts, tourism growth raise concerns for Canada Strong Pass return
articles.summary: The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews. The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a…

image.caption: Banff has seen increased visitation in recent years with or without the Canada Strong Pass, which is set to return for a third year in 2027. (John Gibson/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews. The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a record 4.5 million visitors.
'Free admission should not come with fewer services,' says union
The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews.

The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a record 4.5 million visitors. It provides free admission to Parks Canada sites over the summer.

“I think it’s really commendable, but it needs to have better strategy to go along with it, and currently we’re lacking the strategic part of implementing this really well meaning initiative,” said Banff Mayor Corrie DiManno.

She said the municipality has pushed to have the pass in off-peak seasons such as October and November or March and April. She said other ideas are free entry after 5 p.m., promoting public transit and carpooling, and only giving Canadians free entry.

items: Lake Louise, Moraine need new approach to tourism, says Parks Canada. What that looks like is still unclear

blocks.text: The specific dates haven’t been announced, but the federal budget stated the pass would return this summer.

Parks Canada is receiving $76 million for estimated lost revenue from free entry and discounted camping. The federal agency received about $160 million for the previous two summers and one winter the Canada Strong Pass ran.
DiManno said its return was “quite the surprise and shock” since Parks Canada is expected to reduce its resources in early 2027.
“We’re definitely concerned these budget reductions could have an impact on services that visitors and residents really rely on,” she said.
Parks Canada cuts coming in 2027

Jean-Michel Lavergne, the president of the Union of National Employees, which represents most Parks Canada staff, said it’s important for people to visit national parks. But he said increasing visitations while removing staff is a contradiction.

“If free admission brings more visitors, it means more maintenance, more demands for information and greater pressure on facilities,” he said. “Our members on the ground are really worried how they’ll be able to offer the same services with less people.”
As directed by Prime Minister Mark Carney, 10 to 15 per cent of savings from federal ministries, agencies and departments are expected in the next three years.

items: Rescues in the Rockies cost millions each year. Who pays for them?

blocks.text: For Parks Canada, that means about $145 million in cuts.
The federal agency sent out 2,917 letters to employees — more than half of Parks Canada workers — that their jobs could be cut or their roles changed.
LISTEN | The federal government is bringing back the Canada Strong Pass, but not everybody is happy about it:
Calgary Eyeopener7:51The federal government is bringing back the Canada Strong Pass, but not everybody is happy about it

Lavergne said the union has been meeting with Parks Canada biweekly, but there remain unknowns. Parks Canada staff have until Nov. 23 to take a voluntary retirement or buyout. Lavergne said the union requested an extra 30 days to allow staff to get more information on the changes, which Parks Canada denied.
He said Parks Canada staff take pride in welcoming visitors, but “free admission should not come with fewer services.”
“Our members want to welcome more visitors, but they need the resources to do it properly.”
Banff townsite consistently busy in summer
According to statistics from the Town of Banff, 1.77 million vehicles entered the townsite in July and August — an all-time high.
In 2022, the last year personal vehicles could travel to Moraine Lake, there were an estimated 700,000 visitors.
With more than 200 commercial vehicle operators, Parks Canada estimates visitation now hits about one million people a year.
Lake Louise also remains busy. Parks Canada estimates about 3,300 people visit daily in personal vehicles and about 2,700 on buses.
Roughly half of the visitors on buses are Canadians, according to Parks Canada.

In a statement from the Department of Canadian Heritage, spokesperson Martine Courage said the pass’s return is meant “to make it easier and more affordable for Canadians to explore this country and enjoy its cultural, historical and natural treasures.”
She said it also coincides with Canada’s 160th anniversary.
Courage said the summer was picked since “most children and youth are out of school and have more time to visit cultural institutions and attractions or travel domestically.”
The pass also provides youth with free or discounted access to national museums and galleries, and VIA Rail tickets.
A spokesperson from Parks Canada's national communications team didn't get back to CBC News before publishing.
Banff National Park turns 140 years old

DiManno isn't convinced the increased traffic to Banff is thanks to the Canada Strong Pass — she said summer is peak season no matter what. She noted Calgary and the surrounding area are growing, and increased costs for gas and flights are driving Canadians to travel closer to home.
“It would be great if it can be implemented differently here in Banff,” she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Greg Colgan is a journalist for CBC in the Bow Valley. He was previously the editor of the Rocky Mountain Outlook in Banff and Canmore. He has also worked for media outlets in Ontario and has experience covering topics such as sports, politics, housing and development, courts and arts and entertainment. He joined CBC in 2025. He can be reached at greg.colgan@cbc.ca.
