articles.title: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment
articles.summary: The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

image.caption: A digital reconstruction of the Parthenon's east pedimentImage: Vinzenz Brinkmann und Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann/Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung

blocks.text: The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.
'Very confident we've solved the mystery'

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.
For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.
But now there has been a breakthrough.

blocks.caption: The results of the research are on show at the Frankfurt exhibition 'Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle'Image: Norbert Miguletz/Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung

blocks.text: After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.
The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.
Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.
In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"
Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

blocks.caption: The researchers are convinced that the Dioscuri — the sons of the king of the gods, Zeus — located in Rome’s Piazza del Quirinale are also copies of the group of figures from the eastern pedimentImage: Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: A handy tool: the iPhone

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.
Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.
The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures
There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.
Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

blocks.caption: The landmark of Athens: the Acropolis with the ParthenonImage: Fokke Baarssen/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.
Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.
Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.
The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: William and Kate meet Indian Prime Minister Modi in New Delhi
articles.summary: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which has also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize

blocks.text: Image source, Andrew Parsons / Kensington Palace
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as part of their three-day visit to India.
William and Catherine arrived in New Dehli on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official oversees trip together in four years.
The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.
It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

When he announced earlier this year that it was going to be held in India for the first time, the prince highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
A Kensington Palace spokesperson said ahead of the Modi meeting: "For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage,

"We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level."
The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016.

blocks.caption: Prince William, wearing a black suit, smiles beside Princess Catherine who is wearing a red dress with emerald studs at the 2026 Earthshot Prize in Mumbai, India.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
On Tuesday the prince and princess were in Mumbai to announce the winners of the annual Earthshot Prize.
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
Five separate winners were named during Tuesday's ceremony and each will receive £1m to scale up their projects.

Speaking at the ceremony, Prince William said the 2020s were the time when positive change becomes "irreversible", adding history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
The princess presented on the five awards and, as she did so, said the entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis brought her "hope".

articles.title: India: Online censorship grows after 'Cockroach' protests
articles.summary: Since anti-government Cockroach protests erupted, journalists and creators say their content is increasingly being restricted on social media in India.

image.caption: Digital restrictions have affected independent content creators, journalists and established media organizations, raising concerns about online free speech [FILE: April 2, 2026]Image: Sandeep Singh

blocks.text: A video showing a young girl crying as she spoke about alleged police brutality during the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in July. A video examining the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's (RSS) contribution to the rise of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). A satirical cartoon criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
These are among the examples of content that have recently been restricted on social media in India.
A pattern of restrictions
Content creator CitySavitri describes herself as a "nobody" in the world of social media. She had started making videos just two months ago and had around 600 followers on Instagram.
Yet a video looking at the RSS's role in the BJP's 2014 election victory was restricted in India within an hour of being posted. It was the first of three videos she posted that faced restrictions.
The experience made her feel that "anti-government commentary" was being monitored and curtailed.
"It is very plain and simple to understand," the content creator told DW.
Independent journalist Sadhika Tiwari was covering the CJP protest in New Delhi on July 20, when police used batons and tear gas against demonstrators.
Tiwari's video of a frightened young girl crying and speaking about police brutality garnered around 10 million views within hours, she said, before it was restricted in India.
Political cartoonist Satish Acharya has also faced repeated restrictions, with Instagram blocking his profile twice recently.
'Suppressing independent journalism'

In May 2025, during the conflict between India and Pakistan, independent digital news outlet Maktoob Media's X account was withheld in India while it was reporting on the escalating crisis, its founder and editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told DW.
"We received no official notice or email from either the government or X. It was our readers who first alerted us to the blocking," he said.
Maktoob Media said it contacted Indian officials and X but received no response. Access to the account was restored a few days later, again without an explanation.
Kayyalakkath said Maktoob's content from the July protest also faced restrictions. "Suppressing independent journalism undermines transparency, accountability and democratic values," he said.
Several of the content creators and journalists interviewed by DW said they received no prior notification or explanation for the restrictions.
Some users were not sure if their content had been blocked at the government's request or proactively by the social media platforms.
When asked for comment, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, pointed DW to a website statement noting users can appeal content and account restrictions.
How does the system work?

At the heart of the debate are India's IT Rules, 2021, amended in February 2026. Section 79 of India's IT Act protects social media platforms and other intermediaries from liability for content posted by third parties, provided they meet certain legal conditions.

One such requirement, introduced through the February 2026 amendments, is to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content within three hours of receiving a valid court order or a reasoned government notice. The previous deadline was 36 hours.
Failure to comply can result in intermediaries losing their liability protection.
Censorship in India: Muzzled by the government
The government's Sahyog portal, which coordinates takedown requests between law enforcement, platforms and telecom providers, has faced criticism over the pace at which notices are issued.

Meta said it uses automated tools and technologies to detect and review content that may violate its community standards. It also automatically restricts access to certain types of content in India to comply with legal requirements under the IT rules.

Pranesh Prakash, a technology law and policy adviser, said the amended rules allow authorized police officials to notify intermediaries about content they consider unlawful without necessarily filing a formal complaint or initiating other legal proceedings.

"This has led to the worst period of social media censorship that India has ever seen, with digital news media accounts being blocked, cartoonists' accounts being blocked, and even mere discussions of an opposition leader's memoirs being blocked," he said. "Clearly, none of these disclosed any 'unlawful acts.'"
Prakash also raised concerns about the lack of public information on government requests to remove content, saying this made it difficult to assess the scale of restrictions.
A flaw in the system

The Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in), a digital rights organization, said the growing reliance on automated takedowns raised serious concerns about transparency, accountability and due process.

"There is little transparency about the processes through which content is identified, flagged and restricted, or whether there is any meaningful human oversight before a takedown is implemented," SFLC.in told DW.

The organization also tested X's verification process by submitting a takedown request against one of its own posts using a fake email address. X registered the request, raising questions about how it verified the identity and authority of those submitting requests.
After SFLC.in alerted the company, X introduced email verification codes for people submitting takedown requests.
"A channel that lets anyone pose as a law enforcement official can be misused to silence lawful speech," SFLC.in said.
X did not respond to DW's request for a comment.
Government says no censorship
The Indian government denies that it is censoring online content.

While the ministry did not respond to DW's latest request for a comment, in an email response to DW in August, Vinod Kumar, chief of media and communications at the Information Technology Ministry, said Instagram posts by students and protesters following the July CJP protests "are not being taken down as alleged."
"Media enjoys freedom in India. The Government does not censor online content," Kumar said, adding that the government only acts against "objectionable content."
Under the Indian IT rules, "unlawful content" generally refers to material which could threaten India's sovereignty and integrity, disturb public order, incite violence, or constitute defamation.

However, social media influencers such as university professor Madri Kakoti, alias Dr. Medusa, continue to report restrictions. Kakoti's Instagram account was restricted in India on November 16 without notice, she said, along with that of satirist Shamita Yadav.

blocks.caption: Screenshot of the Instagram account 'the.ranting.gola' showing that the account is not available in IndiaImage: Screenshot Instagram/the.ranting.gola

blocks.text: The price of free speech
Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have warned that expanding content restrictions could chill free expression and encourage self-censorship among journalists, creators and ordinary users.
Acharya, however, said he would continue his work.
"The Indian Constitution gives me the right to draw political cartoons," he said. "It's totally democratic to question and criticize the government in India."

For Tiwari, the issue goes beyond the reach of a single video. It is also about preserving a record of what happened, after the Delhi Police denied allegations of using excessive force during the July 20 protest in front of the Supreme Court.
"We have seen several other videos now, and it's well established why that girl was crying, and that the Delhi Police used force and lied about it," she said.

"Still, I want that video back up because it needs to stay for posterity. I think that's the larger idea: they want to take this stuff down so it fades from memory, allowing them to categorically deny it later when we have little left to show for what happened."
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship

articles.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know
articles.summary: The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

image.caption: Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling withImage: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague.
The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.

Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.
A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.

"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]…. International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.
"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.
Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war
Journey to judgment day

A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.

In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.
Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.
Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.

The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.
A question of intent

As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.

"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.
Bangladesh: Could the UN help the Rohingya return home?
Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.
Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.

Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.
Either-or, maybe both

The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.

"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.

"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.
O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.
Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State, they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.

"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.
Rohingya women in Bangladeshi camps lack toilets
Justice denied vs. delayed
The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.
"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.
"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.
The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.

The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.
What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.

Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.
Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.

"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

articles.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
articles.summary:
Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas supplies

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.

The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.

Analysis by London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.
InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.
“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.

“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”

InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.
That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.

For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.
Of those members assessed, 69% backed stronger climate policies than the BCA, a gap that widened to 78% on energy transition issues.
Herring said the BCA does not disclose who sits on its internal climate and energy committees, obscuring how its policy positions are formed.
“We obviously do know who’s on the association board, but beyond that, there’s no transparency around those internal committees,” he said.

A spokesperson for the BCA said the association supported the “national goal of achieving net zero by 2050 and the setting of interim targets, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy and ensuring we don’t undermine our international competitiveness along the way”.
“The BCA has long advocated for gas as an essential part of the net zero transition – ensuring grid stability – while we move to greater reliance on renewable energy,” the spokesperson said.
The BCA declined to comment on the makeup of its climate and energy committee.
after newsletter promotion
‘Technology agnostic’

The analysis comes as industry groups ramp up lobbying over the “safeguard mechanism”, Australia’s main policy for curbing emissions from its largest industrial facilities, which is under federal review.

While the BCA and most big resources companies publicly support the Paris agreement and Australia’s net zero 2050 carbon emissions target, they interpret what those commitments require in radically different ways to what is widely regarded as climate best practice.

Several oil and gas producer members, including Woodside, argue that increased gas supply is required to support the shift to renewables and enhance energy security in language that has been adopted by the BCA.

This rubs against those BCA members aligned with the findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which found greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure were more than enough to push the world beyond its climate goals.

InfluenceMap also found that the business council frequently lobbies for a “technology-neutral” or “technology agnostic” energy transition, which is the same language used by the fossil fuel sector designed to steer renewable energy funding toward gas.

Persephone Fraser, the ethical research and climate policy lead at fund manager Australian Ethical, said misaligned lobbying was a significant risk for companies and their shareholders, and a major risk to the economy.
“Companies must be scrutinising what is being advocated for in their name and actively correcting the record when it is inconsistent with their own positions, and interests,” Fraser said.
“Membership of an industry association cannot mean outsourcing responsibility for climate lobbying.”

articles.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
articles.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.

blocks.text: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
Dario Amodei

blocks.caption: Dario Amodei wears a grey suit and patterned tie flanked by bodyguards.

blocks.text: Image source, Finn Gomez/Getty Images
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

items: Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile

blocks.text: Daniela Amodei

blocks.caption: Daniela Amodei wears a jacket and sits in an offfice

blocks.text: Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown

blocks.caption: Tom Brown stands on a stage in front of a US flag wearing a dark suit and tie.

blocks.text: Image source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark

blocks.caption: Jack Clark stands on a stage wearing a suit and shirt

blocks.text: Image source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan

blocks.caption: Jared Kaplan wears a biege teeshirt and sits on a stage talking into a small headset microphone

blocks.text: Image source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah

blocks.caption: Chris Olah wears a dark suit and striped tie, and speaks into a microphone sitting in a comfy chair.

blocks.text: Image source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left Toronto University early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish

blocks.caption: Sam McCandlish wears a suit and tie

blocks.text: Image source, Anthropic

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

articles.title: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
articles.summary:
Israeli diplomats say decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large…

blocks.text: Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”

blocks.caption: Palestinian Bedouin boys play football in Jabal al-Baba, near Ma’aleh Adumim, in the area marked for the E1 settlement. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian Bedouin walks up a hill in Jabal al-Baba, where development of the planned E1 settlement will displace several Bedouin communities. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
after newsletter promotion

Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism. If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing. Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

articles.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
articles.summary: Bahrain says it was also attacked by Iran following a US air strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Gulf on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

articles.title: AI a ‘growing concern’ at ASEAN’s parliamentary org, but no concrete measures yet
articles.summary: 'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

blocks.text: ADDRESS. House Speaker Bojie Dy delivers a speech at the opening ceremony of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly General Assembly in Manila on November 18, 2026.
AIPA Philippines 2026 on Facebook
'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

items: The ASEAN parliamentary body is increasingly concerned about the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and the need for a collaborative regional approach to address its challenges.
While the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly can influence member states to adopt regional commitments, any resolutions passed are non-binding and cannot enforce legislation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The persistent threat of artificial intelligence (AI) is a cloud hanging over the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but uncertainty remains over any concrete measure to approach the subject.

“It’s a concern for everybody, it’s a growing concern, and I think it cannot be addressed by one country. It has to be a concerted effort among the regions and other countries to be able to make sure that this is not abused,” House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, head of the Philippine delegation for the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly, said on the sidelines of the AIPA on Wednesday, November 18.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,” House Speaker Bojie Dy, current AIPA president, also said in his opening speech.
Hernandez, however, sidestepped questions about whether a resolution on AI was being drafted during the AIPA general assembly, but said any effort will be “patterned on what transpired in the ASEAN.”

In 2025, the ASEAN adopted a declaration in Kuala Lumpur establishing an ASEAN AI Safety Network, a regional mechanism aimed at promoting collaboration among member states and addressing cross-border AI risks.

AIPA, as a regional parliamentary bloc, is not as powerful as the European Parliament. Any resolution passed during the general assembly is non-binding, which means it cannot force member parliaments to pass legislation back home.
AIPA, however, can still exercise influence by encouraging member parliaments to adopt regional commitments in their own countries.

Concerns about AI come as the Philippines’ hosting of ASEAN was met with massive protests against the US-led initiative Pax Silica, which will lead to the construction of a 1600-hectare AI industrial hub in New Clark City. The project is feared to displace hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers, according to Human Rights Watch.
Only Singapore and the Philippines are ASEAN signatories to the Pax Silica initiative so far. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us
articles.summary: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

blocks.text: What happens when the people you inherited a business with are also the people you can no longer work with? You can quit a job, sell your shares, or find a new business partner. But what if that partner is your brother, sister, cousin, or parent, and the company is something your grandparents spent their lives building?

I have covered Philippine business families for most of my journalism career, interviewing relatives locked in battles over ownership, leadership, inheritance, and family land. Some disputes were already playing out in court, while others were waged quietly behind closed boardroom doors even as the companies kept running. As the feud between cousins Federico “Piki” Lopez and Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III unfolded this year, I found myself returning to those stories, my interview notes, and reading Harvard Business Review research on why family businesses fight and how some survive. In June, I joined family-business adviser Enrique Soriano in an online forum with business owners across Asia to discuss why even wildly successful dynasties break apart.

The Lopez cousins are hardly the first wealthy family to face this problem. India’s Ambani brothers split up the Reliance empire their father built, while the Ortigases fought over control of their real estate business. In Singapore, a father accused his son of trying to take over the board of one of the country’s biggest property developers. Some families eventually called a truce. Others decided they could no longer be business partners, and still fought for years, burning through cash on lawyers and leaving the next generation to clean up the mess.
All of this brought me back to one big question: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

For decades, the Lopez name has been tied to some of the Philippines’ most famous companies: ABS-CBN, Meralco, Benpres (now Lopez Holdings), First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. The businesses changed over time, yet the family stayed connected to an empire their elders built, lost, won back, and rebuilt.

Under Oscar Lopez‘s leadership, the family published Phoenix, a book about how they bounced back from hard times. Piki wanted a different symbol for the next chapter: not the phoenix, which rises again after being destroyed, but the butterfly, which transforms into something completely new. He has also talked a lot about compounding, the idea that smart decisions made consistently over decades pay off far more than quick wins. In his September speeches to stockholders, he stressed that “direction matters more than speed,” pointing to the group’s decision ten years earlier to stop building coal-fired power plants even when coal was still making good money.

That mindset explains Piki’s game plan for First Gen’s energy investments. He believes the company must prepare for a power market that relies more and more on renewable energy. His cousins have questioned whether the bets he’s making are worth the massive price tag, risks, and years of waiting. They have also challenged his authority to make those calls on his own. Gabby and his allied cousins wanted something very different: immediate cash flow and shared family stewardship over a distressed media mission—ABS-CBN—that could not afford to wait until 2031 for long-gestation hydro projects to pay off.

blocks.caption: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Piki Lopez’s town hall as cousins rally for ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The fight turned public and personal. In April, majority owners of Lopez Inc.—representing three of the four branches of the family—accused Piki of acting “like a king without accountability,” questioning First Gen’s deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure, including selling control of its natural-gas business and investing in water-pumping hydropower projects. The majority group later called the hydropower bet “a horrible deal.” First Gen pushed back on those claims, defending the business logic, pricing, and board approvals behind its deals.

The cousins reached a ceasefire in May, but it didn’t hold, and by August, Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc., the private holding company sitting at the very top of the family empire, to businessman Ramon Ang for about P11.56 billion. Meanwhile, ABS-CBN lined up fresh funding. Piki then locked down control of the boards of Lopez Holdings and First Philippine Holdings (FPH), the two companies that hold the group’s stakes in First Gen and geothermal giant Energy Development Corporation (EDC). In November, FPH approved the proposed P15.92-billion sale of its 90.74% controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Gabby’s branch’s investment firm, Crème Investment Corporation, a deal that is still waiting to close. (READ: What it took to save ABS-CBN)
Taken together, these deals suggest the cousins are moving toward a future where they no longer have to agree on how to run the same businesses.
But is splitting up actually better than staying together?

One family owner wants bigger cash payouts today, while the relative running the company wants to plow back those profits into growing the business. Another thinks they should sell the company while buyers are offering a good price, while someone else wants to save it for the grandkids. One wants to ride out an industry slump, convinced a struggling business will bounce back, while another wants to stop pouring money into what looks like a sinking ship, especially when that cash could fund a different business that takes years of heavy spending before turning a profit.

Yet each walks away believing the others are greedy, reckless, or unreasonable. The real trouble starts when the people around the boardroom table aren’t just ordinary investors, but siblings who grew up competing for their parents’ and uncles’ attention, cousins who feel their branch of the family sacrificed more, or heirs who remember the founder’s wishes differently.

Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer, who advise business families and write for Harvard Business Review, explain how everyday business arguments turn deeply personal. In Why Fights Erupt in Family Businesses, they show how fights over money, power, and status get tangled up with family history. An argument over company spending can bring back old resentment over unequal treatment. A fight over who gets to be CEO can reopen old arguments about favoritism. Selling a company might look like a smart opportunity to one relative and a betrayal of the family legacy to another.

Soriano raised another complication during our webinar: many family businesses stay united for decades simply because one strong founder or family elder can settle all the arguments. Relatives might not like every decision, yet they accept the leader’s authority. Once that leader passes away, the next generation realizes it has inherited not only the businesses, but also old disagreements that were never truly resolved.

The Lopezes had larger-than-life leaders in Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr. and his brother Oscar, who died in 1999 and 2023, leaving their successors to figure out how to own and run surviving empires without those strong elders around to settle arguments.
Other Philippine families have ended up in far messier wars.

Take Banco Filipino, once the country’s biggest savings bank, famous for its slogan, “Subok na Matibay, Subok na Matatag (Tested Strong, Proven Stable).” Founded by Tomas Aguirre in 1964, the bank was shut down by the Central Bank in January 1985 before reopening in 1994 after the Supreme Court ruled the Central Bank had abused its power. But its headaches were far from over. It kept clashing with regulators over financial aid, its money troubles, and the fallout from its first shutdown.

blocks.caption: BANCO FILIPINO. This spread in Newsbreak’s March 3, 2003 issue shows the late Don Tomas Aguirre (left) and his children, Ana Marie Aguirre-Koruga (upper right), and Albert “Bobby” Aguirre (bottom right) on a polo field. Rappler

blocks.text: At the same time, the Aguirre family was tearing itself apart from the inside. I covered the legal fight involving Ana Maria Aguirre-Koruga, a minority stockholder who sued the bank’s directors in 2003, including her own brother, Albert Aguirre, who was then vice chairman. She accused them of risky banking practices, conflicts of interest, and shady loans meant to enrich insiders. The directors denied the claims. In 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in Koruga v. Arcenas that her complaints belonged with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), not a regular trial court. That ruling only decided who had authority to hear the case, not whether her accusations were true. The bank shut down for good on March 17, 2011, under BSP orders. The state deposit insurer, Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, took over a bank with 62 branches, 173,480 accounts, and P17.8 billion in customer deposits. The family and regulators kept arguing over who was to blame. While the sibling feud wasn’t the sole reason Banco Filipino collapsed—its financial and regulatory problems ran much deeper—the family war played out inside a bank holding the life savings of thousands of ordinary Filipinos.

The Ilusorio family feud got even more personal. Potenciano “Nanoy” Ilusorio built a multi-billion-peso empire anchored by prime real estate, the pioneering satellite firm Philcomsat, and the exclusive Baguio Country Club. But by 1999, his six children had split into rival camps over their parents, the family fortune, and who should be in charge. When Nanoy grew old and frail, some of his children took him under their care, prompting their mother, Erlinda Kalaw-Ilusorio, to sue them for allegedly keeping her husband away from her, a battle the Supreme Court dismissed in 2001 as the “sad tale of a prominent family shattered by conflicts on expectancy in fabled fortune.” (READ: What drives people to declare war against their own flesh and blood?)

Even Nanoy’s death in June that year didn’t stop nearly 300 civil and criminal lawsuits filed between the rival camps, and according to an account Soriano published in 2016, some children only found out of Erlinda’s death four days later, leading to separate funerals. At one service, the urn reportedly held Nanoy’s ashes because another branch of the family kept Erlinda’s. Another service reportedly barred three of the sisters at the door with security guards.
A fight that started over money and power had reached the point where children could not even mourn their parents together.

In other prominent Philippine clans, the fracture began not at a parent’s deathbed, but when siblings began questioning how a brother or sister was managing inherited assets—turning boardroom suspicions into criminal complaints and proxy wars.

For the Jacintos, who built their wealth in steel, banking, and real estate, also fought over their inheritance. After their patriarch, Fernando Jacinto died, his children clashed over how family properties were being managed and sold. Musician and businessman Ramon “RJ” Jacinto stepped in after relatives questioned real estate deals handled by their sister Marilene, who was running parts of the family business. One fight centered on a large property in Misamis Oriental sold in 2007 for P226 million, which RJ’s camp argued was far below its appraised value. Another involved a Novaliches property reportedly worth about P300 million. Acting as president of family-owned Oregon Land Inc., RJ accused Marilene of faking a deed to transfer the land. Prosecutors charged her in 2012 with falsifying public documents, an accusation that led to criminal proceedings, though not a conviction. The feud showed how inheritance fights can quickly spiral into claims of betrayal and criminal charges between brothers and sisters. (READ: Shaping the future: Family legacies)

blocks.caption: Family feud: Court ruling saves Olivia Yanson’s share in PH’s biggest transport fleet

blocks.text: In the Yanson family, the trigger was a boardroom ouster over who would run the business. They parents founded Vallacar Transit Inc. and the Ceres bus empire, considered among the largest bus conglomerates in Southeast Asia with about 5,000 buses ferrying 700,000 to 850,000 passengers in routes across Visayas and Mindanao regions. In July 2019, four siblings—Roy, Emily, Ricardo Jr., and Ma. Lourdes Celina Yanson-Lopez—tried to oust their youngest brother, Leo Rey Yanson, from running the bus group. Their mother, Olivia Yanson, sided with Leo Rey and Ginette, splitting the family into Yanson 4 and Yanson 2 camps. They fought over who had the right to elect board directors and run the company, triggering lawsuits and battles over company records. In 2025, the Supreme Court said Olivia was mentally sound when she executed her will that designated the Yanson 2 camp as the righful heirs of their family business empire. The family still hasn’t reached the kind of broad peace deal needed to put the feud behind them. (READ: Yanson family feud gets uglier as court brands 4 siblings ‘fugitives from justice’)

This family drama resonated elsewhere in Asia where South Korea’s Lotte Group—the retail, hospitality, and confectionery giant behind Asia’s largest department stores, luxury hotels, and iconic snacks—became the stage for a succession war between brothers Shin Dong-joo and Shin Dong-bin, sons of founder Shin Kyuk-ho. The business giant had major operations in both Japan and South Korea. Dong-joo, the older brother, was prominent in Japan, while Dong-bin ran much of the Korean side. After Dong-joo lost top posts in Japan in late 2014 and early 2015, the brothers erupted into a public war over who had their father’s blessing and who should lead the empire. Their elderly father was pulled straight into the crossfire. At one point, Shin Kyuk-ho backed his eldest son, prompting Dong-bin’s camp to question whether their father was still mentally fit to make decisions. The brothers battled through shareholder votes, lawsuits, and press statements, turning their father’s mental health and legal guardianship into a court case. Dong-bin eventually won over shareholders and kept control, though Dong-joo kept fighting him. Instead of splitting the empire in two, one brother walked away with control of the main group.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: The Shin feud proved a hard truth: being the founder’s son, even being the oldest, doesn’t guarantee inheriting the throne.

In Singapore, the Kwek family— the powers behind iconic skyscrapers, luxury condos, and over 160 hotels worldwide—showed how quickly a disagreement between a father and son could move from the family boardroom into the headlines. In February 2025, City Developments executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng accused his son, chief executive Sherman Kwek, of attempting a boardroom “coup” by bypassing governance rules to appoint independent directors, prompting the elder Kwek to go to court to fire his son. Trading in City Developments shares was suspended as the confrontation became public. For a listed property developer, the dispute raised questions that went beyond the relationship between father and son: Who had the authority to appoint directors? Were corporate procedures being followed? And could the company continue operating effectively while its chairman and chief executive were fighting?

Yet the confrontation ended relatively quickly. On March 12, 2025, City Developments announced that the court proceedings had been settled and would be discontinued. Kwek Leng Beng remained executive chairman and Sherman remained chief executive, while the two newly appointed independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute, Jennifer Duong Young and Wong Su-Yen, stepped down. Singapore’s Straits Times later reported that trusted family friends and senior figures had helped mediate the truce. The company continued under the same family leadership, although the settlement did not necessarily mean that every personal disagreement had been resolved.

Here in the Philippines, the Ortigas family—the landed dynasty behind Ortigas Center and Greenhills—also managed to save its core property business after years of infighting. At stake was OCLP Holdings, which controls prime Ortigas land, Greenhills Shopping Center, and Tiendesitas. To gain an edge, rival branches teamed up with competing giants: the Rafael Ortigas group with Ayala Land, and the Francisco Ortigas group with SM Prime Holdings. The battle spilled into court over board elections and whether nominees tied to a rival developer could hold seats.

Those divisions let Ayala and SM deepen their footholds in a fractured enterprise. In November 2014, the developers and Ortigas factions dropped their lawsuits and agreed to work together. The family kept its landholdings intact rather than carving them up, though peace came at a steep price: bringing in powerful giants handed outsiders major influence over an empire that had belonged to the Ortigas family for generations.

There are strong business reasons to keep a family group intact. Companies under common ownership can share cash, talent, bank relationships, and leadership, allowing a stronger sister company to help a struggling one survive a rough patch or undertake massive investments too large for one branch alone. There is also the pull of family history, where a business built by a grandfather means far more to his grandkids than an ordinary stock investment, making a sale feel like erasing part of the family identity even when the financial math makes sense.
Yet keeping a company together merely because the founder wanted it kept together can create another problem: What happens when the next generation no longer agrees on what the business should do?

Adviser Josh Baron has argued in Why Family Businesses Need to Find the Right Level of Conflict that avoiding disagreement is actually unhealthy. Families must debate tough questions rather than letting owners quietly stew over decisions they feel powerless to change. When relatives can still negotiate and compromise, staying together preserves huge value. But when every investment, dividend payout, job appointment, or asset sale becomes another war for control, the cost becomes far too high.
India’s Ambani family decided that the brothers were simply better off running different companies. (READ: Timeline: Key dates in India’s Ambani brothers’ dispute)

After founder Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002 without leaving a will, his sons Mukesh and Anil fought publicly over who would control Reliance Industries—India’s largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning petrochemicals, refining, telecom, and retail—until their mother, Kokilaben, stepped in to broker a June 2005 peace deal. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries and its core oil and chemical operations, while Anil took charge of telecom, power, and financial services. But it didn’t stop every argument as the brothers later fought over natural-gas supply deals in a battle that reached India’s Supreme Court. Still, they no longer had to agree on every single investment or management call.

India’s Bajaj family—one of the country’s oldest business dynasties, famous for putting India on wheels as a motorcycle, scooter, and financial services powerhouse—also split up its companies among different branches after years of fighting. Under a 2008 settlement, Shishir Bajaj’s branch took control of businesses like Bajaj Hindusthan and Bajaj Consumer Care, while other family branches kept the group’s core auto, finance, and industrial companies.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: Splitting up let each branch follow its own game plan. Their paths quickly diverged: the core Bajaj businesses boomed, while Bajaj Hindusthan struggled with heavy debt and a tough sugar market. Dividing the empire ended the fight over who was in charge, but it didn’t guarantee that both sides would win.

In Hong Kong, Walter Kwok was pushed out as leader of Sun Hung Kai Properties—the real estate titan behind the city’s tallest skyscrapers, luxury malls, and housing estates—in 2008 after clashing with his brothers Thomas and Raymond over how to run the empire. The battle pulled in their mother, Kwong Siu-hing, and tangled up the family trusts. Walter lost his executive job, though he didn’t lose his financial slice of the family fortune. He went on to start his own property company, Empire Group Holdings, while new trust rules spelled out each brother’s share of the family wealth.

Taking a different path is the Murdoch family—the real-life inspiration behind HBO’s hit drama Succession, and the media dynasty behind Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and major outlets across the US, UK, and Australia that have shaped elections and public debate for decades. After a court battle over the family trust controlling voting power in Fox Corporation and News Corp, a September 2025 settlement locked in Lachlan Murdoch’s future control. His three older siblings from 95-year-old Rupert Murdoch‘s first two marriages—Prudence MacLeod, Elisabeth Murdoch, and James Murdoch—walked away with huge payouts and exited the trust. Grace and Chloe, Murdoch’s two youngest daughters from his third wife, Wendi Deng, stayed on as financial beneficiaries under the new setup, but without the voting power given to Lachlan.

Each of these families handled their split differently. The Ambanis and Bajajs divided up operating companies. Walter Kwok stepped out of management while keeping a financial stake. The Murdochs rewrote who holds voting control over their media empire. None of them offers a one-size-fits-all recipe for solving family feuds.

blocks.caption: ADVICE. Enrique Soriano, family business consultant of the Wong & Bernstein  Group, speaks during a forum. Courtesy of the Wong & Bernstein Group

blocks.text: Enrique Soriano, who has advised business families across the Philippines and Asia, does not view such separations as failures, noting during our June webinar that relatives who can no longer work together are often better served by an orderly division of business interests so they can stop being business partners without stopping being family.

Of course, that is much easier said than done. A family deciding to split still has to agree on who gets what, how much each company is worth, who takes on the debts, and what happens to shared properties. One relative might want out, only to find the others can’t afford to buy their shares. Another might want to keep control, but has to bring in an outside investor to help pay for the buyout.
And a peace deal that satisfies the relatives doesn’t automatically work out for the everyday public investors who also have money riding on those companies.

The Lopez cousins appear to be heading toward a more permanent split of their business interests, though whether that turns out well for their companies, outside stockholders, and the family itself will take years to see.
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

Other business dynasties offer no easy answers: The Kweks and Ortigases found ways to keep their shared businesses intact after fierce battles, though both had to make major compromises. The Ambanis and Bajajs carved up their empires. The Kwoks and Murdochs separated day-to-day control from financial ownership. The Shin brothers’ succession war left one brother running Lotte, while the Aguirres, Ilusorios, Jacintos, and Yansons showed how family fights can spiral into years of lawsuits and lasting broken relationships and personal wounds.

There is a world of difference between keeping a company together because the owners actually agree on its future, and keeping it together just because nobody wants to be blamed for breaking up the family empire. There is also a difference between splitting up to chase new ambitions and splitting it up just to stop a fight.

For the Lopezes, going their separate ways may give each branch the freedom to focus on what it values most. Piki can concentrate on long-term energy bets, while Gabby and his allies can focus on lifestyle-related consumer and media businesses. Yet, that freedom brings new pressures, and success will depend on the choices each side makes next.

A family can survive a corporate divorce. Its companies might even grow stronger because of it. Or the split could leave both sides worse off than before. But the real question isn’t just whether relatives should stay together or go their separate ways. It is whether the businesses, and all the people who depend on them, will actually be better off afterward. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Corruption is in gov't DNA -- Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Corruption is in the government"s DNA Vice President Sara Duterte said in a social media post on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 7:20pm
Corruption is in the government’s DNA Vice President Sara Duterte said in a social media post on Wednesday.

In a Facebook post showing her attendance at the 52nd Philippine Business Conference and Expo ng Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) in October, Duterte said that Filipinos dream of a better future.
“Ngunit, malaking hamon sa pangarap na ito ang korapsyon na humahadlang sa atin sa pag-abot ng mas maraming oportunidad at sa kaunlaran,” Duterte said in the social media post.
(However, a big challenge to this dream is the corruption that blocks us from reaching more opportunities and progress.)
“It is a progressive disorder that has embedded itself deep within the DNA of the government—and tragically, it is the Filipino people who are left to suffer the consequences,” she added.
Duterte said as citizens, people should help each other reach that dream, adding that everyone had individual responsibilities.

“As citizens, we have responsibilities, too— to obey the law, reject corruption, protect our communities, participate in our democracy, and demand accountability from those who govern. Nation-building is a shared responsibility,” she said.

Duterte is currently the subject of an impeachment trial where she stands accused of having P817 million to P1.5 billion in unexplained wealth. She also allegedly failed to divest from businesses and did not declare her assets.

She and her defense team have denied all the charges against her. The Vice President has repeatedly cried foul on the corruption allegations, accusing the administration of political persecution. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News
