articles.title: Over 200 ASEAN protesters ordered released from Camp Bagong Diwa
articles.summary: More than 200 protesters have been ordered released by the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office following their arrest during a protest caravan amid the opening of the 49th Association of Southeast…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 18, 2026 7:17pm
Supporters and advocacy groups gather outside Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City to decry the detention of over 200 ASEAN protesters on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. GMA News image

More than 200 protesters have been ordered released by the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office following their arrest during a protest caravan amid the opening of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits in Pasay City.
According to a report Wednesday on GMA News' What We Know So Far, the Muntinlupa prosecutor's office issued the release order following the protesters' detention for the past three days.

The marchers have been held at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City after they were apprehended on Sunday, November 15, during a protest action slamming the planned US-led Pax Silica initiative and the presence of US President Donald Trump in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.
Activists and various sectoral groups have sounded the alarm over the potential risks of the Pax Silica project on the environment, as well as on the indigenous people it may displace.
The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) has already decried the mass detainment, noting that there were reports of minors being among those apprehended. Some protesters were also noticeably wounded.
The CHR also said that its lawyers and investigators were also initially denied access to the Muntinluipa protestors at Camp Bagong Diwa. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: NASA Voyager 1 probe believed to have reached ‘light-day’ milestone
articles.summary: Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance

blocks.text: VOYAGER 1. An undated artist's concept shows NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft.
NASA/JPL-Caltech/Handout via Reuters
Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance

items: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, approximately 16 billion miles, marking a significant milestone in space exploration.
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object and continues to send back scientific data from interstellar space, including measurements of magnetic fields and cosmic rays.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space.

The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday, November 18, at 5:16 am ET (1016 GMT).

Officials at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday, November 19, to discuss the milestone.
“Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter ‌interstellar space ⁠in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018.
A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years.

“But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen,” the JPL representative said.

Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system’s two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space.

“Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager,” Dodd said.
The Deep Space Network is NASA’s international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions.

“After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur,” Dodd said.

“We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond,” Dodd said. “Where does the sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Japanese PM visits Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae laid a wreath on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 7:16pm
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae laid a wreath on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Wednesday.
Takaichi is in the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, where she participated in several meetings with other world leaders.

“On November 18, commencing at 10:50 a.m. local time (11:50 a.m. Japan time), for approximately 10 minutes, Ms. Takaichi Sanae, Prime Minister of Japan, who is visiting the Philippines, visited the Heroes’ Cemetery and laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan said in a short statement.
According to the Armed Forces of the Philippines, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is dedicated to unidentified soldiers who died in the war.
It lies at the center of the Libingan ng mga Bayani with a simple plaque saying “Here lies a Filipino soldier whose name is known only to God.”
The statue serves as a monument where government officials and dignitaries would often conduct wreath-laying ceremonies.

“More than a monument, it stands as a solemn reminder of the countless Filipino soldiers whose identities may have been lost, but whose courage, sacrifice, and service to the nation will never be forgotten,” the AFP said in an X post in August.
During the Japanese occupation of the Philippines in World War II, thousands of Filipino soldiers and civilians were killed.
Japanese soldiers forced 70,000 to 76,000 Filipino and American soldiers to march 100 kilometers in what is now known as the Bataan Death March.
While historical accounts vary, thousands of soldiers died during the march due to hunger and exhaustion. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft claims the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

blocks.text: Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:

items: Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught
Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".

blocks.text: Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.
In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.
"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.
"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."
In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".
In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.
"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.
"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."
Analysis: Potentially the decisive intervention
For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.
Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.
His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.
In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.
Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.
It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?
Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.
Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

articles.title: Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail
articles.summary: As Nigeria's January 2027 polls inch closer, a spate of violence and political thuggery during campaign rallies and town hall meetings is raising concerns about the safety of citizens participating…

image.caption: There are growing concerns over rising political violence ahead of the January 16, 2027 electionImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering.

"I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.

Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.

During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."

blocks.caption: Observers say political violence could deter some voters from coming out to cast their ballot on election dayImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: He was left in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.

As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.
Election-related violence on the rise

Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja.

Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.

Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation.

On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwanso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.

Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.
Nigeria's history of electoral violence

Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria.

Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."

Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.
Peter Obi: 'I will not lose' — but can he deliver?

The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.

"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.
The high cost of violence

A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."

blocks.caption: The 2023 election saw the lowest voter turnout since Nigeria returned to democracy in 199Image: Sunday Alamba/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority.

However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.
"Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.

Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more to the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

articles.summary: Thursday's meeting between the leaders of US, China and Russia will give Vladimir Putin a big stage - but it does not bring him closer to winning the war in Ukraine.

blocks.text: The meeting hasn't even happened yet.
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.
Whatever the outcome.
Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.
That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.
It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.
That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.
But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.
One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.
In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."
But what of those who are not at the table?
Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.
"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.
Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.
Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.
The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.
It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.
The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.
It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

articles.title: Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?
articles.summary: El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible…

image.caption: Inside El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT). Image released by the El Salvador presidential press office following its inauguration in 2023Image: Press Secretary Of The Presidency Of El Salvador/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.

These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.

More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.
What is a mega-prison?

De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.

But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.
High costs and a questionable track record

According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.

It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.

Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.

Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.

However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).

The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.

"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe. As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.
Security, propaganda and human rights

Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.

However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.

Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."

blocks.caption: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele's hardline approach has included mass arrests, a prolonged state of emergency and the construction of the country's massive CECOT prisonImage: Jose Cabezas/REUTERS

blocks.text: Can the Salvadoran model be exported?
Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.

Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.

However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.
What are the alternatives?

In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.

In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.
Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.

Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.
This article was originally published in Spanish.

articles.title: Investing in AI Literacy Means Investing in Judgment
articles.summary: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or
articles.byline: Angel Chiang, Jewel Zhu, Paolo Miguel Ordonio

blocks.text: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or how it can serve other people. These questions are part of AI literacy, alongside an understanding of the technology itself. Helping people make such judgments requires education that connects AI with their circumstances and responsibilities.

For Break the Fake Movement in the Philippines, this work builds on its focus on media and information literacy and countering disinformation. In a March 2026 research interview with the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society (CAPS), co-author Paolo Miguel Ordonio, Break the Fake Movement’s executive director, explained that its AI education emphasizes foundational understanding and critical thinking, and its curriculum includes ethics, copyright, data privacy and safety. He described enthusiasm for AI that does not always translate into understanding, alongside communities where some learners still need help with basic digital activities.

Different audiences also bring different needs. At the time of that interview, Break the Fake Movement was exploring how to adapt its AI literacy training for civil society workers through a collaboration with the Association of Foundations. Modules developed primarily for young people, parents and educators provided a starting point; understanding what civil society workers needed from AI education was part of the adaptation.

For civil society workers, AI literacy needs to address decisions they face at work: which problems AI can help solve, which tasks it can support, and where human judgment should remain central. CAPS’s report, Cars Without Roads: Investing in AI for Good Across Asia, illustrates the kinds of decisions people may face. Organizations approaching Infoxchange with plans to adopt AI sometimes discover that they first need better data management, stronger cybersecurity or a clearer definition of the problem they want to solve. In a separate CAPS interview, Hyomi Ahn, a researcher at Korea’s Beautiful Foundation, described its work to develop internal AI guidelines. She also highlighted debate among advocacy organizations about whether AI should draft public statements, raising questions about which work should remain human.

AI literacy programs can be designed for staff and leaders alike, with learning adapted to their different responsibilities. Staff may need to judge how AI fits their tasks; leaders may need to learn how to set expectations, develop guidance and provide time and resources for staff learning. The report’s findings on organizational readiness suggest that this education should also help people recognize when specialist advice is needed and what support colleagues need to apply their learning.

Yet funding for literacy education can be difficult to secure. Drawing on Break the Fake Movement’s experience, Ordonio described limited funding opportunities for literacy education, saying that funding favored infrastructure, tools and systems. His experience reflects the report’s wider concern that human capability and supporting conditions receive less investment than visible applications. In the study’s pre-interview survey of 36 organizations, 72.2% of respondents identified training and capacity-building as underinvested, the highest share for any category and more than double that of any other area.

blocks.caption: Executive Ordonio delivering a lecture on AI usage for parents.

blocks.text: For funders, this means supporting AI literacy programs that adapt learning to participants’ responsibilities and provide opportunities to consider where AI fits their work, whose needs it serves and what responsibilities its use entails. Funding this learning recognizes informed judgment as a capability worth developing and an essential part of turning technological possibilities into social value.

articles.title: Barbers urges probe into alleged detention of Sara Duterte aides
articles.summary: House prosecution panel adviser Ace Barbers has called on authorities to investigate allegations that two household helpers of Vice President Sara Duterte were detained and forced to sign a document…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 6:06pm

House prosecution panel adviser Ace Barbers has called on authorities to investigate allegations that two household helpers of Vice President Sara Duterte were detained and forced to sign a document against their will.
Barbers made the call after Duterte’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo, said the two household helpers were already safe and sound with assistance from the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

“This should be validated because this kind of incident should not happen. Dapat kasuhan natin kung sino man yung mga gumagawa niyan, dahil isa ‘yang krimen. Hindi dapat pinalalampas ‘yan,” Barbers said at a press conference.
“They should report it to the PNP or the NBI,” he added, referring to the Philippine National Police and the National Bureau of Investigation.
Barbers urged the complainants to seek government protection once they file a complaint, calling on law enforcement agencies to investigate and hold those responsible accountable.
“Once they are able to file the complaint, we urge the national government and all its agencies, law enforcement agencies to protect the complainants and go after the perpetrators,” he said.
House prosecutor Joel Chua of Manila also urged the two household helpers to file a complaint so those responsible could be held accountable.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the South China Sea Code of Conduct?
articles.summary: The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 6:04pm

The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues — but what is it? And what is taking so long for the involved nations to agree?

While conflict in the South China Sea has had tense confrontations between China and the Philippines, parts of the contested waters have other claimants, including Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Brunei.

According to the ASEAN's website, member state parties and Beijing agreed to issue the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) in 2002 to maintain peace in the disputed waters.

The agreement stated that all parties are seeking peaceful resolutions to their maritime disputes to ensure regional stability. In 2011, the Guidelines for the Implementation of the DOC was established, which further reinforced the declaration.

"The Parties concerned undertake to resolve their territorial and jurisdictional disputes by peaceful means, without resorting to the threat or use of force, through friendly consultations and negotiations by sovereign states directly concerned, in accordance with universally recognized principles of international law, including the 1982 UN (United Nations) Convention on the Law of the Sea," the DOC read, referring to the UNCLOS.

Also known as the Law of the Sea Treaty, the UNCLOS is the international agreement that defined the limits of the territorial seas of nations and the areas in which they could exploit marine resources. It also established the rules for the use of the high seas for international navigation, and outlined the rights and responsibilities of nations in the protection of the marine environment.

The UNCLOS served as a legal basis for the Philippines' case against China before an international tribunal in The Hague. The case was filed in 2013 and won in July 2016, junking China's nine-dash line claim over the South China Sea, but Beijing has been steadfast in refusing to recognize the ruling.
Years of negotiation

As for the DOC, the countries also agreed to practice self-restraint when conducting activities that could escalate disputes or affect stability, including occupying uninhabited islands, reefs and other features.

The DOC stated that the parties concerned reaffirmed "that the adoption of a code of conduct in the South China Sea would further promote peace and stability in the region and agree to work, on the basis of consensus, towards the eventual attainment of this objective."
It is this code that has taken years to negotiate.
According to the ASEAN website, discussions over the COC began in 2018 when the first draft was established. However, the undersigned countries have failed to reach an agreement.
Over the weekend, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said the COC was about 80% finished, but salient issues remained.
She said the COC is likely to be finished in 2027. The DFA originally wanted to finish it by 2026, which would have coincided with the Philippines' chairship of the ASEAN.
Negotiations and China
While Lazaro did not dive into what the salient issues are, doubts have been raised about China's sincerity in establishing the COC.
The late former foreign affairs secretary Albert del Rosario said in 2014 that he doubted that China would work quickly for a legally binding COC.

"I'm not very optimistic about whether China is serious about an expeditious conclusion [of a Code of Conduct] because I can see the aggressive provocative acts that we are seeing now and which is, I think, is their way to pursue an expansion agenda," Del Rosario said.
The South China Sea, or the West Philippine Sea for areas within Manila's 200-km exclusive economic zone, has been a point of contention between Beijing and Manila for years.
Tensions have considerably risen during President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s term, with the present administration making a stronger claim over its maritime territories. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: [DECODED] Scam season and the leaks that may make it worse
articles.summary: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

blocks.text: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

items: With only 37 days until Christmas, holiday preparations are causing increased traffic in Metro Manila, coinciding with the recent ASEAN Summit.
A GSMA survey reveals that while many Filipinos are aware of scams, with 76% expressing concern, scams continue to evolve, including new methods like 'quishing' via QR codes.

Recent data breaches have exposed personal information from various government agencies, prompting warnings about increased scam risks during the holiday season and highlighting the need for better public awareness and reporting mechanisms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

There are only 37 days before Christmas! Have you started your holiday preparations already, and are you feeling the Christmas rush yet? I’ve noticed that Metro Manila traffic has been heavier over the past week, although that may have been due to preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which just wrapped up.

Between the traffic and the shopping, the holidays are when we’re busiest and least careful, especially with our transactions. A recent survey by the global industry trade organization GSM Association (GSMA) said that Filipinos do know the risk: 76% said they “absolutely worry” about scams and 78% said they changed their behavior due to scam awareness.

And yet, scams still proliferate — and they have been evolving along with technology. Smishing (SMS phishing) has been in the public consciousness for a while now, but have you heard of quishing? It essentially does the same thing, except that it’s done via QR codes.

Rappler researcher Lourence Angelo Marcellana listed 12 types of scams to watch out for, as we approach the holiday season. He also explained how to protect yourself against scams, especially since much of our transactions now happen online, thanks to the growth of e-commerce and digital payments.

In the GSMA report, it said that the Philippines also has the highest rate — among Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam — of reporting scams to digital platforms (49%), compared to only 16% reporting to the police. The regional average of reporting scams to the authorities is at 36%.

This reminded me of a Decoded study we did last year on online scams. We found that government agencies were among the most active sharers of warnings online, but because each agency’s approach lacked coordination with the others, the overall effect on consumers online was dissatisfaction from all the fragmented messaging.

Users online also complained about the government hotlines set up for reporting scams, saying that they found them difficult to use and lacking a clear process to submit evidence and receive updates on their cases.
That was last year. This year, the problem has now moved from how well the public is warned to knowing what kind of personal details may already be exposed, and who might be using them.

Last Friday, November 13, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) confirmed that personal data from around 20 state agencies were exposed in recent data breaches. Rappler researcher Alex Culla looked into these agencies and listed the personal information potentially exposed, from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission, to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

Among the personal details that may have been compromised are names, addresses, email addresses, mobile numbers, birth dates, genders, and even taxpayer identification numbers (TIN). Of course, these vary depending on the agency, and not everyone who deals with these agencies is necessarily affected. But it’s still worth staying alert, because while scams do happen all year, the CICC said it might become more prevalent as the holidays approach.
So if these recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start. At Rappler, Christmas isn’t the only thing we’re counting down to.

This year’s Social Good Summit is taking place this Saturday, November 21, and it will include a masterclass on data privacy and personal safety in the age of AI. There will also be discussions on technology, journalism, and human rights, as well as masterclasses on vibe coding, editorial cartooning, and crisis management.

articles.title: Wait for the most common diagnostic scans in Manitoba 'worse now than it ever has been': doctor
articles.summary: Doctors and patients say a diagnostic wait time crisis is putting people's lives at risk, as the highest number of Manitobans on record wait for scans that help diagnose brain tumours, heart disease…

image.caption: Big Daddy Tazz, a well-known Winnipeg comedian, paid $950 for a spine MRI in British Columbia after he was told he would likely wait a year for one in Manitoba. Without that test, 'for another year, I would've waited for the results, to find out that I could be doing something to relieve myself of s

blocks.text: Doctors and patients say a diagnostic wait time crisis is putting people's lives at risk, as the highest number of Manitobans on record wait for scans that help diagnose brain tumours, heart disease and other potentially deadly medical conditions.
The number of people waiting for CT scans and ultrasounds in the province now surpasses the wait caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the province's diagnostic wait time data.
Over 45,000 people in the province were waiting for an ultrasound as of August 2026, compared to an average of 16,000 in 2019 — the furthest back the province's publicly available data goes.
Almost 29,000 were waiting for a CT scan in August (up from 8,000 in 2019), and 18,000 for an MRI (up from 15,000).
"It is worse now than it ever has been," said Dr. Fourie Smith, a family physician who has practised in Manitoba since 1998.

Earlier this month, Winnipeg comedian Big Daddy Tazz paid for a private magnetic resonance imaging test, which creates images of structures inside the body, after he was told he would likely wait a year for a spine MRI to help diagnose pain that was shooting up his arms and legs.
"I was afraid if I didn't pay for this MRI, that if we were on the wrong track and I did the wrong thing for a year, that I would do more damage," he said.

items: Do you have a tip about Manitoba's health care system you want to share? Send your tips in confidence to iteam@cbc.ca or call us at 204-788-3744.

blocks.text: The standup comedian paid $950 for a private MRI in Kelowna, B.C, where he has a second home.

He learned he has a pinched nerve tunnel in his spine and a condition that was putting pressure on his spinal cord. He doesn't need surgery, but the test gave him a path for how to treat his pain through stretches and exercise.
Without the test, "for another year, I would've waited for the results, to find out that I could be doing something to relieve myself of some of the pain," he said.
Big Daddy Tazz paid $950 for a private MRI, a medical imaging test that creates images of structures inside the body. (CBC)

A CBC analysis of the province's diagnostic wait time data found that depending on where the scan is sent, Manitobans can wait nine months or longer for an ultrasound, 15 months for a CT scan and 10 months for an MRI.

Manitoba family doctors say those waits are putting them at a breaking point, where they struggle to make the best medical decisions for their patients when the answer is reliant on a diagnostic image that could take a year to receive.
Demand outpaces staffing: union
The province tracks the median number of weeks a person waits for a scan from the time a requisition is sent to a facility to when it was completed.

At Grace Hospital, the median wait for a CT scan is over a year, according to the Winnipeg hospital's August data. That means half the people waited less than a year for a CT and the other half waited longer.
At Misericordia Health Centre in Winnipeg, patients waited nine months for an ultrasound.
While the MRI waitlist has improved from 2025, when times ballooned and over 28,000 people were on the list, patients are still consistently waiting 10 months or longer.
Dr. Michel Bruneau, a family doctor in Lac du Bonnet, says he sometimes won't even bother ordering an MRI because he knows the wait will make it useless. (Gary Solilak/CBC)
Dr. Michel Bruneau, a family physician in Lac du Bonnet, northeast of Winnipeg, said he often just skips ordering an MRI, because he knows the wait will be so long the test won't be of any use.
"By the time they get their [scan], the damage is done, and you can't do anything about it anyway if you wait six months," he said.
Since 2019, the average number of CT scans done in the province has increased by 38 per cent, while MRIs have increased by 23 per cent and ultrasounds by 11 per cent.
But the union that represents the technologists needed to do those scans says staffing rates have not kept pace.

items: Northern Manitoba mobile MRI unit parked in Thompson, struggling to keep staff, associations say

blocks.text: The number of full-time equivalent technologist positions has only slightly increased since 2019, according to the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals. Union president Jason Linklater says it's time for Manitoba's NDP government, in office since 2023, to create a human resources strategy to meet the demand.

Dayna McTaggart, the Manitoba provincial manager with the Canadian Association of Medical Radiation Technologists, says the increased demand for scans stems from an aging population, increased disease monitoring and more patients with family physicians.

Dayna McTaggart, the provincial manager of the Canadian Association of Medical Radiation Technologists of Manitoba, says the demand for diagnostic imaging has been steadily increasing. (Submitted by Dayna McTaggart)
The association warned governments that increase was coming for years, yet "we haven't seen an equal increase in the growth of the profession," said McTaggart.
Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara echoed McTaggart's point on doctors, saying that because the province has hired more physicians, there will be more referrals.

The solution is "to train the right number of people to deliver these tests and scans," the minister said, pointing to a mobile MRI unit that recently moved to The Pas to start doing testing in northern Manitoba.
'Crisis for physicians': Doctors Manitoba
Dr. Smith, who is the medical director of Winnipeg's Dakota Medical Centre, said the situation has become so dire he is constantly forced to decide which of his patients he can help move up the list.
He can only ask radiologists for a priority slot so many times, he said.
"Imagine being put in that position where I have to decide between case A, B and C, when I'm going to pick up the phone and make that call," he said.
The doctor said he can’t pinpoint exactly when things got so bad, but said it began in the last two years.

items: MRI waits surge in Manitoba after nearly 2 years of NDP governance

blocks.text: The province proactively publishes a wait times dashboard that gives an average median wait time for procedures, using data from all facilities. That means in calculating median wait times, the nine-week wait for an MRI for a child at Health Sciences Centre is given the same weight as the 10-month wait for an adult MRI at HSC.
Those median times also do not capture how long it can take for the scan ordered by the doctor to be processed by the province's central intake system and put in the queue.
That can extend the wait by up to three months or longer, say Dr. Smith and Doctors Manitoba — the advocacy association that represents over 4,000 physicians.
The intake system used by Shared Health, Manitoba's provincial health agency, relies on a digital fax system.
That means "if we say that the wait times in Manitoba is X, it's actually significantly worse than that, because that referral lies. … waiting to get processed," Dr. Smith said.
Doctors Manitoba surveyed 68 physicians who said 78 per cent of their requisitions take over a month to get acknowledged by intake.
Manitoba government urged to tackle record diagnostic wait times
One doctor noted a requisition took six months to process before it was rejected for missing details. Others reported requisitions going missing.
More than 60 per cent of the doctors surveyed said the increased wait worsened patient outcomes through delayed diagnoses, poorer health and additional required treatments.
The combination of long waits for tests and the central intake bottleneck have created a "crisis for physicians trying to get their patients the care they need," a Doctors Manitoba spokesperson said.
Central intake has a 24-hour turnaround for urgent scans, but is still processing non-urgent requisitions from August, said a spokesperson for Shared Health.
Minister Asagwara said they recently attended a Doctors Manitoba summit on the issues with the referral process, and they are committed to "axe the fax."

Work is ongoing to modernize the central intake system, Shared Health's spokesperson said in an emailed statement. A casual clerical staffer has been hired to help address outstanding requisitions, they said.
'Not just a number on a piece of paper'
But Smith said the current situation leaves doctors, who have no way of tracking the status of their referrals, wanting "to pull our hair out" with frustration.

There were at least two cases where his office waited a year to hear about a referral and was told by central intake it was sent to a hospital, only for the hospital to say they never received it, said Smith.

Lac du Bonnet's Dr. Bruneau said he sees the consequences of the wait times with his dementia patients. A brain CT scan can help diagnose the cause of the dementia and lead to treatment — but waiting a year delays the ability to do that.
"In that year, that person with dementia has often declined significantly," he said.

Big Daddy Tazz said he grapples with what he describes as survivor's guilt because he got an MRI immediately, knowing many others can't afford that option. That's one reason he's speaking up, he said.
"This needs addressing," said Tazz. People on waitlists need to know the province cares, he said.
"We're not just a number on a piece of paper. We are human beings that are terrified."

articles.title: Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.summary:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of…

blocks.text: Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

blocks.caption: A man cries during a protest in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, condemning violence against Rohingya people in Rakhine state, Myanmar. Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPA

blocks.text: The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu at a joint news conference in the White House last year. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
after newsletter promotion
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

blocks.caption: Palestinians search for bodies and survivors among the rubble in a destroyed area after Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, in October 2023. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA

blocks.text: In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: ‘Phantom forests’ in Australia’s arid outback used to create carbon credits meant to offset emissions, report claims
articles.summary:
Carbon credit companies reject research that found only small increase in forest and canopy cover in regeneration areas despite wet conditions

  • Get our

blocks.text: A fight over the legitimacy of Australia’s climate change policy has reignited after researchers claimed “phantom forests” in the semi-arid outback are being used to create offsets that allow fossil fuel companies to keep pumping out pollution.

A group of academics, including professors from the Australian National University and the University of New South Wales, said they had examined 50 forest regeneration projects used to create carbon credits.

Led by Prof Andrew Macintosh, the former federal government carbon credit scheme integrity chair and the director of ANU’s Centre for Environmental Markets, the researchers said they found only a small increase in forest and tree crown cover in the areas over the past five years despite wet conditions.

They said the conclusions were consistent with their previous peer-reviewed studies that found Australia’s method for creating carbon credits from forest regeneration was doing little to nothing to help address the climate crisis.

The research was published in a report released on Wednesday by the Australian Conservation Foundation. Prof David Eldridge, one of the report’s authors and a former principal research scientist with the NSW environment department, said he was “gobsmacked” that “phantom forests” in outback areas north-west of the remote town of Bourke could earn carbon credits for forest regrowth.
“Some of these areas have never grown forests; they will never grow forests,” he said.

The findings were rejected by companies that manage what are known as human-induced regeneration projects in north-western NSW. “These are some of the most closely examined carbon projects in the country, and the evidence on the ground shows they are working,” a spokesperson for Green Collar, a business that manages carbon credit projects, said.
Each carbon credit is said to represent one tonne of emissions that has been removed from, or prevented from being released to, the atmosphere.

Their use is contentious, in part, because industrial-polluting companies that are required to cut emissions under a federal policy known as the safeguard mechanism are allowed to buy an unlimited number of credits to count as their own cuts while continuing to pollute.
Scientists have warned limiting the climate crisis requires rapid direct cuts in emissions and that carbon credits – also known as offsets – should be used sparingly.
The Australian Conservation Foundation said it showed coal and gas companies should be banned from claiming offsets as their own emissions cuts.

Adam Bandt, the foundation’s chief executive and a former Australian Greens leader, said the safeguard mechanism was meant to “cut climate pollution and protect us from big coal and gas threatening our lives and livelihoods, but it’s not working”.
“Putting more climate pollution into the atmosphere now could push us past dangerous tipping points. It can’t be offset, and the science tells us to keep coal and gas in the ground,” he said.
Macintosh said the evidence showed the projects were by and large not regenerating forest, but had created more than 60m carbon credits worth up to $2bn.
after newsletter promotion

The report said the safeguard mechanism was being “materially undermined” by poor-quality credits. It said a “flood of cheap, low integrity” credits was making it cheaper in many cases for big polluters to pay for offsets rather than make direct emissions cuts.

There have been more than 430 human-induced regeneration projects in Australia since 2013, covering an area of 38m hectares – larger than Japan. The federal government is now reviewing the safeguard policy, as required under legislation.

A spokesperson for the Clean Energy Regulator, which manages the scheme, said it took allegations about the integrity or efficacy of carbon credit projects seriously, and had confidence in the forest regeneration method.
It said projects were required to demonstrate every five years that canopy cover was increasing, and it had rejected non-complying areas that could have received 6.7m carbon credits.

Green Collar said it stood “firmly behind the integrity of its human-induced regeneration projects” and expressed frustration that the report had not been publicly released or published in a peer-reviewed journal. It said the researchers had “judged these carbon projects with satellite pictures and a single field visit”.

“Carbon is stored in stems, branches, leaves, roots and dead timber. Satellite canopy products see leaves from above. They do not measure the wood and roots where most of that carbon sits,” its spokesperson said.

Skye Glenday, the chief executive of Climate Friendly, another carbon credit project developer, said the criticisms of the carbon credit projects were “at odds with the facts and the extensive independent scientific and regulatory scrutiny that is applied to all projects”.
“Debate about the use of offsets is legitimate, but let’s have that debate on its merits rather than undermining the carbon drawdown Australia also needs,” she said.

articles.title: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
articles.summary: Tyler Buchanan, from Dundee, was a member of the notorious Scattered Spider group and began hacking when he was a teenager.

blocks.text: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.
They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.
Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.
